lal.summary: Anyone (besides Phil) still worried about Kobe after he shot 28 percent from the floor in the preseason? Anyone else surprised to learn that Kobe's Lakers have won a league-leading six straight road openers?

Favorable schedule or not, this has been some opening statement from the defending champs ... Pau especially. So much for starting slowly, Kobe's supposed advancing age, saving their legs for the playoffs Celtics-style, etc.

It's not just two straight L's that dropped the Lakers two spots. It's how they lost. Giving up 239 points in the past two games without going into overtime in either one, specifically. After all that nationwide slobbering.

The schedule has indeed been cakey. The defense, by Laker standards, has been spotty. The champs, though, are back to crushing people, as evidenced by the league's only current double-digit average scoring margin.

Wondering why the Lakers can't crack the top two? Must have escaped you that the champs are in the midst of their second losing streak and have feasted on teams with a combined record of 83-131 in their 13 wins.

The annual Kobe Shot Watch has begun after the champs snoozed to four straight L's. As ESPN Stats & Info informs: L.A. is 8-0 when Kobe takes fewer than 20 shots, 4-3 when it's 20-24 and 2-3 when it's 25 or more.

Never imagined having the champs out of the top five at any point, let alone for two straight weeks. No alternative, though, when L.A. -- having played the league's easiest schedule so far -- is 4-4 in its past eight games.

The champs, believe it or not, were not a slam dunk to rejoin the top five. They have one win -- ONE -- over teams with winning records (Bulls). Combined record of the six teams they just beat on the road? Just 54-108.

Imagine trying to three-peat without home-court advantage in the second round, conference finals or Finals. That's how L.A.'s playoff road looked Monday morning  without having played any of our top three teams yet.

No flow on O. Their transition D is AWOL. Three of the worst four home Ls in Pau Gasol's nearly three years as a Laker have been witnessed just since Christmas. Can't pin all that on mere boredom/complacency, can we?

How much has this 6-1 surge and Dallas' struggles without Dirk helped the champs' collective psyche? That's still the big question in Lakerland, where team tension was more discouraging than the anticipated boredom.

Even with their recent offensive resurrection and seven straight wins before they lost Sunday's Staples scrap with the Clippers, I'm not sure that the champs would be back in the top five if injuries hadn't derailed Dallas. You?

More data to suggest that West's No. 1 seed is already out of reach: Kobe and Co.'s second-half schedule would appear to be unavoidably tougher, thanks to a league-low 13 games so far against teams at .500 or better.

The slow-looking champs are 1-5 in Kobe's last 35-point games and 1-5 against the teams (San Antonio, Boston, Chicago, Miami and Dallas) with the five best records besides theirs. But it's just the regular season, right?

So many of the Lakers' big names were in the news last week that this tweet boast from the injured Matt Barnes almost went unnoticed: "No team can beat us in a seven-game series" when L.A. is "health[y] & focused."

No one ever says much about the galvanizing effect of the Lakers' annual Grammys Trip, but this one had a real Rodeo Road Trip feel until L.A. followed up its Boston breakthrough by breathing life into Orlando's season.

The concern is not that Kobe played too hard and burned up more precious fuel Sunday night. The concern is that he went so hard after the All-Star MVP nod because he secretly fears it's the only trophy he can win.

Help at the deadline would have been handy, but a W in OKC -- even with Perkins out -- gave the champs six quality road wins in February, which is progress even when you account for what happened in Cleveland.

Everyone who said that the Lakers have too much size and too much Kobe to worry about their various periods of malaise during the first 50-odd games ... we can hear you revving up your Told You Sos from here.

Wish I had a dime for every time I heard this on press row Saturday night: Bet the Lakers are glad now that they didn't trade Bynum. And the rich get richer: L.A. doesn't have to play another road game until April 1.

The Lakers held off Portland, sure, but Bynum's suspension halts the best run of his career. Drew just reached double digits in rebounds in seven straight games, after getting there just 10 times in his first 39 games.

Only three times in the last 10 seasons has the team with the best record after the All-Star break won it all. The way that the reigning champs have been rolling, that amounts to a ray of hope for the rest of the field.

If anything's deeply wrong with Pau or Bynum, then the Denver loss obviously meant more than the committee (of one) has decreed. If not? An L the Lakers -- universally re-established as title faves -- can live with.

It's hideous for the champs -- who in the worst case could suddenly fall all the way to No. 4 in the West -- but L.A.'s latest siesta is great for playoff intrigue after that 17-1 run made them seem so invincible again.

mia.summary: LeBron, D-Wade and Bosh have only managed to shoot a collective 44 percent from the field. And it hasn't even mattered since the opening night trip to Boston because the Heat's collective D has been so smothering.

Getting tweets galore from giddy Bosh bashers saying we should've seen his struggles coming. That we overrated him. Say what? No one pegged Bosh to lead the Heat in scoring, but who didn't expect him to rebound?

The Heat's six wins, in case you missed it, came against teams (Sixers, Magic, Nets twice, Wolves and Raps) that are a combined 16-32. The teams (Celtics twice, Hornets and Jazz) that inflicted Miami's four losses: 22-5.

Not expecting much sympathy out there for the Miami Hurt, but the committee (of one) can plainly say we're not enjoying this. Can't expect anything from them while Miller and Haslem are out and Wade is hobbled.

The number of Cavs questions lobbed at LeBron this week in advance of his first game back in Cleveland just got slashed. A 9-8 start, rumblings of player dismay with Spoelstra and Bumpgate surely took care of that.

A handful of Heat fans are asking why the Lakers aren't subjected to the same crisis talk as Miami when the champs have also lost in Memphis and at home to Indy. Simple answer: Rings almost always get you pardoned.

On what should we focus? The eight straight wins by double digits? The combined 75-112 record of the victims? The faster pace? A resurgent D-Wade? Or LeBron's congratulatory tweet to Akron U.'s men's soccer team?

Know this as you study up for Miami's full-circle showdown with Dallas: Fastbreak points looks like the key stat in any Heat box score. When they score at least 15 in transition, they're 12-2. Fewer than 15? Just 9-6.

How do you go 14-1 after starting 9-8? A softer schedule certainly helps, but so does this: Miami is allowing nearly eight fewer points per game (from 94.5 ppg to 86.7 ppg) and grabbing nearly six more boards nightly.

How did the Heat become the first team in history to go 10-0 on the road over the course of a month? Stifling D and a resurgent D-Wade were the two keys next to LeBron's ridiculous December: 25.2 ppg, 7.9 rpg, 6.8 apg.

The Heat have lost just once in their last 22 games ... and once in the last 43 days to be as precise as possible. So it seems safe to suggest that the Heatles, if nothing else, have at least figured out regular-season basketball.

Have to factor in LeBron's injury last week, but the fact remains that the Heat's blemish is a 4-8 mark against the rest of our top 10 ... although they still haven't played two residents: Oklahoma City and San Antonio.

Still wondering, nearly a month later, if Spoelstra was referring to the committee (of one) when he said: "You can get whiplash if you really follow you guys and your opinions game to game." Nah. Couldn't have been us.

There's always a lively debate in ESPN.com meetings about what close games really tell us, but something tells me Miami was sweatin' at 1-8 in games decided by five or less (worst in the league) before the weekend.

Although it's not quite revenge without Durant in the building, Bosh made a tough-guy stand Sunday, holding Blake scoreless on 0-for-5 shooting. Against every other Heater, Blake had 21 points on 7-for-12 shooting.

Losing in Boston, with so many circumstances seemingly in their favor, dropped the Heat to 1-6 against the Celts, Bulls, Mavs and Lakers. Worse yet: Cleveland has more W's against the Celts than Miami this season.

LeBron's 29 points, 12 rebounds and 10 assists Sunday night add up to just the second triple-double in All-Star Game history. And just like Mike in '97, it wasn't enough to deliver an All-Star Game MVP trophy. Tough crowd.

Continually losing big games will continue to hurt the Heat here every Monday, but memories of 2006 still haunt those of us who wrote them off that season for being just as bad or worse against the elite. 'Til it mattered.

Spoelstra will surely come to regret letting any of this slip, but the tale about crying players did divert some of the focus away from Miami's crunch-time failings and that 1-9 mark against teams from the .700 Club.

Did dropping the Heat all the way down to No. 9 trigger the ferocious response that dragged them past the blazing Lakers and/or spark the subsequent throttling of the scorching Grizz? You see it, too, huh?

The Heat salvaged a 5-6 record from that killer 11-game stretch despite losing the first five of those games. They're suddenly up to 20-20 against teams with records of .500 or better. They're thrilled, basically.

With seven of their nine games left against teams with losing records -- and knowing how clinical they are (32-5) against the sub-.500 set -- you can't completely dismiss the Heat's chances of snagging the East's top seed.

You'd think that the Heat's humbling return to Cleveland would lead to a steep drop ... until you remember Miami is one of only two teams to beat the Lakers since the Cavs stunned the champs in Cleveland on Feb. 16.

The Heat wound up going 4-9 against the teams with the five best records besides theirs (Spurs, Bulls, Lakers, Celtics and Mavs). Not that it matters as much as we all thought in an East that is winnable for them.

bos.summary: I'm always whining to any coach, GM or scout who puts up with it that PGs today don't know how to pass. So I won't dwell on the L in Cleveland because I want to keep the focus fully on Rondo's glorious dimeage.

It's not just the Lakers making us know-it-alls look silly for suggesting that various title contenders would ease into the season. The Celts are back in the top two after a 4-0 week awash in more glorious Rondo dimeage.
The Celts' only two losses came on the road on the second night of a back-

You saw the worst of the Celts in their past two games. They didn't have Rondo in Toronto, true, but they also played with a lack of focus and respect, first against Durant-less OKC and then in the Canadian matinee.

Delonte's injury is an undeniable blow, but Rondo's return puts our focus back on dimeage, with RR (14.2 apg) attempting to join John Stockton as the only other player in history to average 14 dimes for an entire season.

The Rondo Effect: Folks are starting to ask on a regular basis whether RR can really pull a Stockton and average 14 dimes for the season. The KG Effect: Boston has started a brisk 16-4 for the fourth consecutive season.

Boston still has to guard against another post-Christmas tumble, but if you'll permit a brief follow-up to last week's stuff in this space: No team in history before these Celts had ever started 16-4 in four seasons running.

KG's resurrection. Pierce's clutchness and versatility. Overcoming every injury. The Celts are just overloading us, since we also can't stop reciting Barkley's priceless Rondo line: "He's the engine that stirs the drink."

I knew the Celts had been good before Christmas in the KG era, but I didn't know they were this good until Elias informed us that Boston's 94-14 mark is the best pre-Christmas over any four-season span in NBA history.

Injuries are the obvious issue, but the numbers are still startling: Boston lost seven of its first nine games starting with Christmas 2008, eight of 12 right after Christmas 2009 and three of four starting with Christmas 2010.

Question of the week courtesy of Magic GM Otis Smith: Isn't it possible that the Celts -- not Orlando -- are the ones with matchup issues (with Perkins out) and overloaded on bigs because Dwight is harder to counter?
There's plenty of time to dig into KG's return. Shaq's first 20-point, five-

A second straight road L -- at lowly Washington even with KG back -- generated not-so-surprising rumbles that the C's still dream of luring Sheed out of retirement ... then swiping Rip Hamilton from Detroit via buyout.

Never overestimate one regular-season game. I'd be lying, however, if I didn't admit to hearing voices whisper Doc's trusty line about how his "A" starting five has never lost a series after what the Celts just did in L.A.

Doubt the Celts would rather see the Lakers in the Finals than a Texas team, but check out the teams with the best records in Boston since the C's moved in '95-96: San Antonio (12-3), Houston (10-5) and Dallas (10-5).

Boston has been alone atop the East for a whopping 83 days this season -- compared to Miami's three -- but the Celts' overall deteriorating health (with Pierce hobbling now) makes it impossible for them to celebrate.

The Celts are one of just three teams in the last 35 years to send four players to one All-Star Game. Which is another way of saying they'll find a way to cope even if they lack the trade assets needed to land Battier.

I know, I know: Ainge is a gambler, and re-signing Perk would have been expensive, and Boston has badly needed a 3/4 since Posey left. None of it stops me from saying Boston's trade was more surprising than Utah's.

The new guy looked pretty loose Friday night in our first up-close glimpse of Jeff Green in green. Can't help but wonder, though, if he really realizes how much playoff scrutiny is coming in the Celts' post-Perk world.

Didn't give too much thought -- even after a home loss to the Clips and their defeat in Philly -- to booting the Celts out of the top five. Holding the Bucks to 56 points, however, was a wise way to make sure.

You know the saying: As Rondo goes, so goes Boston. So it's no wonder that the Celts are in a 3-4 funk; Rondo has averaged just 6.0 ppg and 6.4 apg, while shooting 31.3 percent from the floor, in those seven games.

One more time in case you haven't heard it: Friday's collapse against Charlotte marked the first time in Celts history that they fell to a team 10 or more games under .500 after leading by 10 or more to start the fourth.

Honestly can't think of a single one-on-one playoff matchup I want to see more than Shaq versus Dwight. Yet it's impossible not to wonder now, after Shaq's latest setback, whether we'll see him at all in the NBA Tournament.

Maybe it's just me, but I would have expected these Celts to try to rally around Perkins' exile by vowing to spite Ainge for doing the deal. Never expected a 9-10 funk with Rondo failing to reach 10 assists 13 times.

por.summary: The Blazers were right there with the Hornets for Team of the Week status, but there's only one topic on the minds of Blazermaniacs today after the sad, sad news about legendary enforcer Maurice Lucas. R.I.P., Luke.

Latest entry for your next You'll Never Guess What Happened To Portland This Time discussion: The Blazers were assigned to play five games in the second week of the season ... and had to visit the Lakers in game No. 5.

Sometimes you don't want to be right. And this is one of those times. The pessimism about Portland staying healthy toted into the season by the committee (of one) is proving justified before we get to Thanksgiving. Sad.

One of the many sad facts in a city with too many to count: The battered Blazers pulled out two nice Ws last week amid the latest heaps of pain ... but never get the props Houston always did for its success when Yao-less.

Not the best start to Portland's four-game swing through the East: Nate McMillan announces that B-Roy is restricted to 30-35 mpg  ... and a players-only meeting ensues after losing in New Jersey on the first stop.

Don't think even the most fervent Blazermaniacs would deny now, with B-Roy clearly operating at less-than-full capacity and Oden down again, that Portland has slipped out of West's Biggest Threat To L.A. contention.

Say this much for Wes Matthews' Blazers: Even with Roy's mobility perhaps forever compromised and Oden seemingly cursed, these guys refuse to feel sorry for themselves. As Phoenix (twice) and Orlando just found out.

Not sure if he's the first to say it, but the new nickname for Roy, Oden & Co. spotted in John Canzano's column in the Oregonian -- Frail Blazers -- rings as harsh as it is true. Just like Jail Blazers from another era to forget.

We're getting in a mention of Portland's 5-2 record without B-Roy while we can because it won't look that good next Monday if he continues to sit. Four of the Blazers' next six games are on the road, and all six are toughies.

The two wins over the Jazz to close out 2010 weren't just a pick-me-up Portland needed because of all its injury torture. The Blazers were also 0-8 against the rest of the West's top eight before sweeping Utah sans B-Roy.

Another shock to the system after our recent discussion with Camby about the "snake-bitten" Blazers: Wes Matthews responding to his First Trimester MIP nod with a curse-defying 36 points in Friday's win at Minnesota.

Props all around for what's left of the Blazers, who are 11-7 without B-Roy (compared to 10-13 with him) and have Aldridge (one of the NBA's top five bucket getters from five feet and in) scoring inside like never before.

20 No one is coping with life minus Roy, Oden and Camby better than Aldridge, who has quietly joined Blake Griffin, D-Wade, Amare and Dwight Howard as one of the league's top-five bucket-getters from five feet and in.

Very valid question from NBA.com sage Fran Blinebury: Shouldn't the mere fact that he's managed to stay healthy in Portland -- or Chernobyl as Fran calls it -- clinch a spot on the West All-Stars for LaMarcus Aldridge?

The breakdown for the one Blazer seemingly impervious to the league's worst injury plague: Portland is 12-5 when Aldridge scores at least 25, 8-4 when he scores between 20 and 24 ... and 7-15 when he's held below 20.

Maybe it'd be wiser for B-Roy to wait until after the All-Star break to launch his comeback. LaMarcus Aldridge just topped 35 points for the third straight game; Drexler is the only other Blazer who knows that feeling. Ever.

Will be easier to gauge the Blazers' stretch-run prospects after Thursday's deadline, since they'll almost certainly have some new blood by then. They think Aldridge has taken a legit step and they want to make a trade splash.

For all the justified love LaMarcus Aldridge has been getting, he suddenly has something even more satisfying: help. Camby has been reactivated, Gerald Wallace has been acquired ... and B-Roy is back with a flourish.

The Blazers just held Charlotte under 20 in every quarter -- only the fourth time in team history that's happened -- and are riding a 9-3 roll that could be even better. Since all three L's came at home.

Bummed as the Blazers must be to go 2-2 on a trip that began with a Florida sweep, it's still a good time to urge you to stop with the "West is down" talk. Huh? With lower seeds like Denver, Memphis and Portland?

The latest encouraging sign on the heels of Gerald Wallace's arrival and B-Roy's comeback: Nicolas Batum rumbling for 25 points against the Lakers. He'd been way too quiet for a guy so many teams have lusted after.

Some decent trivia from Elias that I didn't see coming: Do you know what Gerald Wallace has in common with Tim Duncan, Chris Webber and Walt Frazier? All of them have five career 40-point games after Wallace's latest.

The Blazers wholly deserve their Team No One Wants To See in the playoffs status. Not just because of years of injury hell but because they took on salary at the trade deadline. Good to see the rare go-for-it teams rewarded.

Sources say there are no back-to-backs in the playoffs. So it seems safe to buy into the idea B-Roy -- like Portland's depth, home-court mojo and versatility since acquiring G-Wallace -- will be a playoff factor.

orl.summary: If you're compiling a list of Week 1 disappointments, Orlando's no-show after halftime in Miami has to top it. Don't try the back-to-back excuse, either, because the win over the Wiz couldn't have been less taxing.

Still thinking, fairly or unfairly, about the beatdown the Magic absorbed in Miami. Perhaps Monday night's reunion with the Atlanta team they abused in the playoffs this past spring will get my mind out of the gutter.

Everyone I know who's been there says Orlando's new arena is spectacular. Sad, then, to see the lethargic Magic christen the place with two quick L's, including Friday's surrender (110 points allowed?) to the Bosh-less Raps.

Looks like both of the Magic's main rivals are going to be sweating health all season. Would love to tell you the Magic have the focus/togetherness to take advantage of such helpful circumstances, but I'm still dubious.

Time to start considering the possibility that those offseason tutorials from Hakeem Olajuwon did make some impact. Howard has scored at least 20 points in six straight games, two games shy of his best-ever scoring run.

That had to be some stomach bug to knock Dwight out for two games. You take for granted how durable the big man is; Howard has played in 507 of Orlando's 512 regular-season games since the start of the '04-05 season.

The latest hint that the Magic are headed for a shake-up that hits harder than the stomach virus that just ran through this team: Orlando's four L's already this month match its total for the whole of December last season.

If anyone in Orlando can feel good about an overhaul this dramatic -- which wouldn't have surprised our loyal readers -- it's the coach. Van Gundy must feel some pride that his bosses imploded the roster instead of ousting him.

Rondo wasn't out there, true, but 15 of the final 16 points in any crunch time against the Celts is, well, something. Way bigger, on this scorecard, than the new guys routing the Spurs on the second night of a back-to-back.

Five straight W's by an average of 14 points catch the eye, but the following development has to hearten Orlando even more: Hedo is already looking more like 2009 Hedo, averaging nearly 15, 5 and 5 during the 5-0 run.

Most interesting element of the Magic's nine straight wins by eight points or more? They've averaged 16.1 fast-break points in those wins. In its first 28 games, Orlando was the league's worst running team at 7.9 ppg.

If you didn't believe that overhauled Orlando has to win a championship to keep Dwight Howard committed to staying in the Magic Kingdom, you're encouraged to visit the Weekend Dime. Answer No. 6 out of 10, specifically.

Magic Kingdom dwellers, please tell us: How much satisfaction did you take Friday from the snippet in Simmons' marathon chat where he said that the Magic "scare me" with Ryan Anderson in the Rashard Lewis role?

For all the justified glee about Ryan Anderson's play as the new Rashard Lewis, Orlando is down a spot to No. 4 in the East since the big trades ... with Arenas averaging 8.5 ppg as a Magician on 36.7 percent shooting.

The Magic were a wobbly 16-9 when they swung their big trades ... and they've slumped to 16-11 since. They're so out of sorts that Dwight, for the first time since December 2006, hasn't blocked a shot for three games.

The most desperate Florida team on Sunday's TV docket? Had to be Orlando thanks to those eight straight L's to teams with winning records. The most impressive Florida team on the dial? Orlando by a mile after beating L.A.

No. 4 in the East, bizarrely, might be where you want to be now if you're Orlando. Forget Boston in Round 2. It'd also likely mean an Atlanta team they know well in Round 1 as opposed to those new wild cards from MSG.

The Magic would be reveling in the departure of Dwight's worst one-on-one nightmare ... except that Boston's willingness to ditch Perkins mid-stream actually suggests that the Celts don't even sweat Orlando any more.

Getting a 16-tech suspension this early, when your name isn't Sheed, has to hurt Dwight's MVP campaign, no matter how impressively he's otherwise carried the load amid all the change and struggles in the Magic Kingdom.

Not what the Magic bargained for: Arenas has taken 659 shots in 2010-11 ... and is shooting 37.5 percent. Only three other players are sub-40 percent with at least 600 FGA: Brandon Jennings, Trevor Ariza and John Salmons.

The good folks at Elias, who keep track of everything, inform us that Jameer's triple at the horn to beat Denver was the season's 15th buzzer-beater and the third from deep (Tyreke and Durant had the others).

This probably speaks more to the ongoing Boston funk and Miami's recent 5-6 stretch against .500-or-better teams, but Orlando actually has the East's second-best record since the All-Star break ... at a modest 11-5.

Dwight's ability to keep the Magic in the top five in defensive efficiency while surrounded by sorry defenders would move me more if Orlando was heavily favored in Round 1 against underachieving Atlanta. Or favored at all.

Just because he's not getting my MVP vote doesn't mean that I won't take a quick 20 to hat-tip Dwight Howard for joining Hakeem, Barkley and Moses as the only players in the last 30 seasons to average 23 ppg and 14 rpg.

atl.summary: Down to four unbeaten teams already and the Hornets aren't the only surprise in that group. The Hawks had to win their first two games on the road to join 'em, posting just the third 2-0 start on the road in team history.

Tell us, America: Disappointed in the Hawks for losing at home to Phoenix in the first game they've played against a team projected as playoff-worthy? Or does a 4-0 road record mean more than whom they've played?

Bizarre coincidence or something more telling? The Hawks are the only team in league history to win their first six games and then lose the next four ... and now they've done it twice in the past three seasons.

Obviously wouldn't have known this without our friends from Elias, but All-Lefty Team fixture J-Smoove is on course to become the fifth player ever to average 16 points, 9 boards, 4 assists and 3 blocks.

We indefinitely suspend all "Highlight Factory" references. The Hawks boast all of two wins over teams with records of .500 or better (New York and Indy) and have five losses at home after seven all of last season.

The Hawks are coping OK so far with life minus Joe Johnson (elbow) ... except for the fact that winning without him only revs up those who believe JJ doesn't make enough of a difference to warrant that $123 million.

Make that 5-2 without the injured Joe Johnson -- including wins at Orlando and at home over Indy to double Atlanta's total against .500-or-better teams -- to keep pests like us asking about the $123 million splashed on JJ.

Think seeing the Hawks win five of their first seven games without Joe Johnson -- with the only defeats coming to Miami and San Antonio -- helped heal him so quickly ahead of schedule after his elbow surgery? We do, too.

This month's wins over Orlando can't change the Hawks' plight. They're the East's fifth-best team at best, fortunate to see the Magic when they were a mess before the big trades and then right after they went down.

The Hawks, for the first time in nine years, won their first game of a new calendar year with Sunday's comeback in Clipperland. Next project? Spruce up that 3-9 mark against .500-or-better teams if you want to move up.

The good news? Joe Johnson is heating up in his return from elbow trouble. The bad news? Atlanta is living off its success against sub-.500 teams (21-5) and is just 4-9 against .500-or-better teams even after winning in Utah.

Even those of us hammering the Hawks for fattening up on sub-.500 teams -- at 22-6 -- can't completely dismiss their 10-game home winning streak. Not when they outscored the opposition by an average of 11.1 points.

One game isn't exactly conclusive, but this didn't hurt Horford's case for Hawk of the Year status: 59 points without Al on Friday night against the Hornets established a new franchise low since the move to Atlanta in 1968.

Joe Johnson couldn't be giving them more than he has in January: 26.0 ppg on 50.4 percent shooting. Who out there, though, sees the Hawks having homecourt advantage in a single round of the playoffs this time?

Some week for the Hawks. They got twice as many All-Stars as I expected (Horford and Joe Johnson) and passed Orlando to move into the East's No. 4 slot right after I suggested they were doomed to No. 5 (at best).

Do the Hawks even want home-court advantage in their seemingly unavoidable first-round reunion with Orlando? Valid question after Atlanta couldn't hold a 22-point lead at Philips Arena against the up-and-down Bobs.

Vibe I get is that the Hawks' interest in a deal for Devin Harris has been overstated. So if the fans' dream of an upgrade at point guard is forthcoming, chances are it'll have to be someone else. Ramon Sessions?

The Hawks have finally injected that roster with some new blood. Snatching the No. 4 seed from Orlando might be their modest ceiling now, but they were heading the other way without the decision to go get Hinrich.

The feel-good factor after that big comeback to topple scorching Chicago didn't last long. The Hawks just became only the third team in Mike D'Antoni's three seasons to score fewer than 80 points against the Knicks.

Sekou Smith of NBA.com, who's been tracking the Hawks for years, did the painful research and calculated that Kirk Hinrich is their ninth PG since the 2005 draft ... when Billy Knight didn't take D-Will or CP3.

Going 3-2 on a six-game homestand entering the finale against Chicago is somewhat understandable given the quality of the opposition. The unacceptable part? Atlanta has topped 91 points three times all month.

Only five East teams have winning records since the All-Star break and this ain't one of them. Philly's home loss to Sacramento helped the disengaged Hawks more than anything they've done lately to help themselves.

No one has frustrated DH12 this season like Jason Collins, as Professor Hollinger expertly explained, which has the Hawks convinced they can beat the team in Round 1 that humiliated them in Round 2 last season. Thoughts?

I know Jason Collins is the supposed Dwight Stopper. I'm also well aware of Atlanta's 3-1 edge in the season series. I just can't forget how uninspired the Hawks, 10-15 since the All-Star break, have looked for weeks.

okc.summary: Will too much be made of OKC's first real test of the season (home date with desperate Utah) resulting in its first disappointment of the season (21-point humbling)? In the world of inflated expectations? Of course.

Will too much be made of the fact that OKC has been beaten at home on back-to-back Sundays with plenty of preparation time in advance of both games? In the world of inflated expectations? You know our answer by now.

Not ready to accept that the burden of h-u-g-e expectations in OKC after carrying Team USA is messing with Durant's shot. Too soon. Admitting concern about OKC's unrecognizable D, by contrast, is totally justified.

Durant shooting 42.6 percent from the floor and 30 percent on 3-pointers? OKC riding the Westbrook Express to back-to-back wins in Boston and Milwaukee sans Durant and with its most stifling D of the season? Huh?

We're down to two players averaging at least 20 points, five rebounds and five assists: LeBron and Westbrook. Which means Durant, amazingly, wouldn't even be voted the first-month MVP on his own team. Right?

Prof Hollinger sums up what I've been trying to say since the season's first rankings: "Fans and media alike got way ahead of themselves" when the "ages of [OKC's] top eight players are 21, 21, 22, 22, 23, 24, 26 and 27."
Friday's courtside seat in New Orleans reminded the committee (of one) that all the fretting about OKC's slippage on D/Westbrook's ability to QB/

Not so surprised to see Grant Hill turn back the clock on the Thunder. The bigger surprise was seeing this season's kings of the close game fail to pull that one out: OKC's now 9-2 in games decided by five points or fewer.

Durant's majestic 44 points against the Melo-less Nuggets, making him the second-youngest ever (behind T-Mac) to score at least 40 on Christmas, can't mask the concern that won't go away: OKC's defense still ain't right.

You knew this season couldn't possibly go as smoothly as last season for the Thunder. And here's more proof: Scotty Brooks has used five starting lineups already after needing just three different combinations in 2009-10.

For all the talk about the Thunder's regression on D, who looks more stable in the Northwest Division than Durant, Westbrook and Co.? Utah, Portland and Denver (and Sota, obviously) would all trade for OKC's problems.

We repeat: For all of OKC's slippage on D and the undeniable need for more size, whom in the Northwest Division would you regard as more dependable or playoff-dangerous than the team with the league's highest-scoring duo?

They've only outrebounded 22 teams this season, compared to 55 last season. Their regressed D gets nitpicked here and elsewhere regularly. But OKC still had four more W's than it did at 2009-10's 41-game midpoint.

Dear KD: Please resist any urge to be your usual impeccable self and retract what you said about Bosh after Sunday's showdown. Let it sit. We all loved this: "Lot of fake tough guys in this league and he's one of them."

Amid the obsession with the Thunder's dips on D and on the glass compared to last season, sometimes we could all do with a little perspective: OKC was mired at 12-38 at the 50-game mark as recently as February 2009.

Ringing up 30 isn't as easy as we make it sound for Durant. He leads the league in 30-point games with 22 and he'd certainly get there more often if it were easy because the Thunder are a robust 18-4 when he cracks 30.

Not the sauciest topic to hit here, but surely worth a mention: Only two teams in history (Boston in '89-90 at 83.2 percent and Dallas in '02-03 at 82.9 percent) have been better at the FT line than this OKC team (82.7).

Can't say it better than Professor Hollinger said it. For three-and-a-half seasons, OKC was a team of the future. After the deals for Perkins and Mohammed and the size they've injected, OKC is a team of the present.

Perhaps Perk delivers everything OKC theoretically lost when it rescinded the Chandler trade two years ago. Yet you can't help wonder here if he's really going to be healthy enough to be a game-changer this season.

It's too late for a real Sixth Man Award push but a welcome development in OKC given that Perkins hasn't logged a minute yet: Harden is averaging 17.6 ppg off the bench since Jeff Green was sent away to Boston.

You can safely assume that the Thunder didn't expect to start 9-1 in March with Kendrick Perkins playing in only three of those games. Just as they never expect to lose at home to the Raps no matter who is or isn't playing.

Don't think anyone in OKC will mind too much at 11-2 in March, but Durant is in the midst of his lowest-scoring month all season (25.1 ppg) and almost never gets mentioned in an MVP race he was widely tipped to win.

What a difference a week makes. From a 14-2 record in March, OKC's April has begun with two road Ls ... and with its lead over No. 5 Denver down to three games before the likely first-round foes hook up twice this week.

Even after last week's sweep of the Nuggets, I still say it's going to be fascinating to watch how OKC handles a Round 1 series with dangerous Denver when expectations, for the very first time, are so sky high.

den.summary: For one Monday, anyway, we shift the comment spotlight from our Melo myopia onto George's storybook return to the bench. Which is just where it should be after a home rout of the Jazz and a nice W at Houston.

We say this not because George Karl is such a loyal rankings reader but because it's true: His Nuggets haven't received nearly enough credit for how hard/well they've played in the face of Melo drama and injuries.

First they surrender a seemingly impossible 54-point quarter to the Pacers. Then, some 48 hours later, they inflict the Lakers' first loss to halt L.A.'s second-best start ever. One of the wilder pendulum swings we've seen.

You tell us, Nuggets Nation. Dismayed by what you're seeing passion-wise from Melo and Co. with the franchise in limbo? Or reasonably satisfied at a game over .500 given injuries to K-Mart and Big Bird?

Four straight wins. Four more to 1,000 career for George Karl. A buzzer-beating dagger against Chicago -- and an attempt to play through illness -- from the allegedly detached Melo. Life is as tranquil as it gets in Denver.

Denver probably can't decide what's more pleasing. Stretching its win streak to a surprising seven? Or temporarily handing the speculation baton back to the Hornets thanks to the chaos surrounding their sale and CP3?

The seven-game win streak is a memory after a l-o-n-g four-game trip ... and the Melo Speculation Machine is cranked back up to full speed after a quiet few weeks. Let's see if the Nuggets are vulnerable. Or numb to it all.

This was easy to miss once Orlando decided to trade away half its team, so it's worth repeating that the Nuggets -- as of Thursday night -- were openly "listening aggressively" to Melo offers according to new GM Masai Ujiri.

The Nuggets are the only team in the league that hasn't lost four straight games in any of the past four seasons. That changes Tuesday with a home L to Portland ... with Melo still likely to be on compassionate leave.

With Melo back from compassionate leave and Al Harrington looking like he might be able to shake off a dislocated thumb and play again as soon as this week, Denver could have its full squad for the first time all season.

Can't knock Denverites for booing what they saw Sunday night. They've been pretty patient sitting through months of Melo limbo, but they're suddenly watching a team that looks fried mentally by the ongoing drama.

Trivia to pass the time: Who was the last player with a scoring average as high as Melo's 23.1 ppg to be dealt in-season? Denver was involved in that one, too, snagging Allen Iverson from Philly in December 2006.

You have to rewind to the Paul Westhead era for the last time Denver had the league's most prolific offense (107.4 ppg). Not that it'll be easy to sustain that with more road games (and Melo's presumed exit) looming.

Although you couldn't tell in Sunday's meek surrender in Philly, Melo has been bringing it more often in January, even with so much drama swirling. He's had five 30-point games, after coming into the month with only seven.

Melo's passive-aggressive stance throughout his trade saga has tortured us all since September, but he's hung around so long that he just might leave behind enough cushion to nab Denver a playoff spot before he goes.

The Nuggets really are this season's drama kings. Only they've won two games on buzzer-beaters after Afflalo followed up Melo's dagger against Chicago with a dagger J of his own to halt the Mavs' 10-game win streak.

Melo leaves Denver as its third all-time leading scorer, with seven straight playoff appearances but only one beyond the first round ... and with everything he was dreaming of: NYC, MSG and that $65 million extension.

With New Orleans getting Landry, Portland getting Wallace, red-hot Memphis getting Battier and Denver keeping all of its Knicks from the Melo deal, maybe the bottom half of the West bracket won't be Pushover City.

Good news: Denver is 5-2 with multiple quality wins since trading Melo and could have won all seven. Bad news: Denver is still tied with Sacramento for the league lead in L's (12) after leading by 10 or more.

Denver is 7-2 since dealing Melo. With five wins against teams with winning records and an average victory margin of thirty-five points in the other two wins. Think OKC is eager to see the starless Nuggets in Round 1?

A deficit of 4 1/2 games is undeniably substantial this late in the season, but are you really ready to say Denver can't climb to No. 4 when it has two games left with OKC and the Thunder just lost at home to Toronto?

The COY ballot is officially impossible thanks to what the Nuggets have done (12-4) minus Melo. George Karl's work, pre- and post-trade ... who's been better? Can't conclusively say Thibodeau, Popovich, whoever.

Maybe there remains a stray question or two about what kind of road team these new Nuggets are ... if you want to nitpick. But they're the NBA's third-best team since the All-Star break (15-4) and an easy choice for No. 3 here.

Probably not the most advisable play to say it out loud, but Denver's only two losses in its last 10 games should help explain why George Karl publicly admitted that he'd rather see Dallas than OKC in the first round.

dal.summary: Remember how the Mavs swore they were lasered in on sprucing up last season's 28-13 home record? It took only two home games for the issue to be reraised thanks to a late meltdown against the Zach-less Griz.

The Rangers couldn't quite close. The Cowboys are suddenly America's Laughingstock. The town is there to be taken ... and the Mavs are averaging 14.0 points and 8.5 turnovers in their past two fourth quarters at home.

No surprise Dirk missed zero time after spraining one of his bionic ankles yet again. Huge surprise, however, that team D has been the Mavs' salvation while they wait for Beaubois' return to give the offense a spark.

Good luck trying to explain why the Mavs, for the second straight season, are so much more ruthless on the road than at home. You called that like you predicted Dallas -- Dallas! -- would be winning games with D.

Seminal week in the Big D: Mavs sweep four games in five nights for just the third time in team history ... and The Sports Guy launches a passionate Dirk4MVP campaign on his podcast that sees us trying to calm him down.

It'll be fascinating to see what The Streakbusters can do with their six straight home games. I'd buy into Hollinger's idea that they can stretch this thing to 15 ... except that the Mavs lose focus at home so often.

The considered view of Dallas-area native Deron Williams after D-Will's Jazz became victim No. 12 in a row: "Best Mavs team I've seen since I've been in the NBA ... by far the best defensive team we've seen from them."

Their win streak and No. 1 ranking are gonzo, but the Mavs still have to feel decent about themselves. First they send Miami straight into that team meeting, then Phoenix makes a huge trade hours after a heavy L in Big D.

Very aware that the Mavs lost on a Monday last time we had them No. 1, and that they're playing Monday night at OKC after a rust-building five days off. None of that can matter when this is where they deserve to be.

Received a tweet asserting that the famed Power Rankings jinx, after the Mavs' rise to No. 1 last Monday, is what caused Dirk's knee injury that night in OKC. Someone out there wants to hurt the committee (of one) bad.

DeShawn Stevenson is the 3-ball-draining MIP candidate who absolutely no one talks about. Then again, let's face it: No one in Dallas wants to talk about anything but Nowitzki's return with the Dirk-less Mavs in a 2-6 funk.

Losing Caron Butler for the season right after Dirk went down robbed Dallas of the Mav best suited to fill in for Dirk as its go-to guy. The result: Dirk's finally back, but a troubling amount of the Mavs' 24-5 momentum is gone.

What keeps the Mavs in the top 10, even after that horrific 3-10 stretch? Their slump-busting victory over the champs means Dallas has W's over every 30-win team (Spurs, Celtics, Lakers and Heat) except the Bulls.

Still not rolling like they were before Dirk and Butler got hurt, but beating the team from DC that can't win on the road would ensure that the Mavs (7-8) avoid their first losing January since going 3-11 in January 1998.
If anyone in Big D feels triumphant after a week of havoc-wreaking, rep-

Barea is en fuego, Peja broke out  in Houston, Beaubois will make his long-awaited comeback this week ... and Caron keeps insisting that he's coming back for the playoffs. Maybe the Mavs really don't need a trade.

One L in 14 games, by one point, has them back to No. 2 in the West over L.A. despite that 2-7 funk without Dirk. We repeat: With Roddy back, Barea scalding and Caron talking playoff comeback, do they even need a deal?

Tough to nitpick a team on a 16-1 roll, but it is a concern that the Mavs -- thanks to their trouble holding leads -- have already played 23 games decided by five or less. That was their season total in Carlisle's first two.

The margins are indeed so ridiculously slim in the ultra-competitive top five that the Mavs losing for just the second time in 20 games (both by just one point) and temporarily losing Chandler causes a two-spot dip.

For all the talk about how much Chandler's presence has changed them, few teams out there can match the Mavericks' innate ability to turn a 20-4 run into a crisis ... because of how painfully they took the four L's.

We were half-joking with last week's crisis talk, but the locals are in a full-blown panic now. After six straight narrow defeats to teams in the West's top eight, no one wants to hear a word about Dallas' recent 18-1 tear.

Caron Butler (knee) continues to insist he'll be back at some stage in the playoffs, but Dallas has an effective replacement if it can keep Peja healthy. How effective? The Mavs are 15-0 when Peja plays at least 15 minutes.

Last week's shoves and barbs have illustrated precisely why we've been clamoring for a Mavs-Lakers series for months. The problem? The Mavs' ongoing 8-8 funk makes it harder and harder to picture them getting there.

How will you remember the season in Mavsland? For the 11th straight 50-win season of the Cuban era? Or the panic-inducing recent nosedive that has turned them into the elite team everyone wants to see in the first round?

sas.summary: Surprises galore from the Spurs already. They rung up 122 points on Indy after topping 120 three times last season, extended Tony way early and watched Timmy manage just seven and seven in a home L to the Hornets.

The Spurs have very quietly injected their roster with some quality youth: George Hill, Blair, Splitter, maybe even sleeper Gary Neal. Which is one big reason we keep saying they might be L.A.'s biggest worry out West.

It says right on the Most Improved Player ballot that the award "is designed to honor an up-and-coming player." But how do you exclude 30-year-old Richard Jefferson if RJ and the suddenly free-scoring Spurs stay this hot?

Focus on the Spurs being in the midst of the eighth double-digit win streak of the Popovich Era? Or the fact that Duncan has five single-digit scoring games already? That didn't happen last season until March.

Stealing this edgy but effective comment concept from friend o' the committee Jemele Hill: How many Hollywood actresses must Tony Parker split up with to get the new high-octane Spurs some media spotlight?

They've won four games Utah-style after trailing by at least 15. Humbled the Hornets on back-to-back Sundays. And they've matched the best 20-game start in team history. So, do we forgive that road L to the Clips?

Portland's Nate McMillan tried to shine some spotlight on the new, runnin' Spurs with Sunday's proclamation that this is "the best team in the league right now." To no avail. Call it the quietest 20-3 start of all time.

The Spurs would be the first to concede that the early schedule has been favorable. Doesn't change the fact that Timmy, Tony and Manu are all healthy/productive/reveling in the energy from their young supporting cast.

It's spotlight time at last for the team that only sports the league's best record: Lakers at home Tuesday, Mavericks in Dallas on Thursday, Thunder at home Saturday  with a trip to Boston looming for the Spurs on Jan. 5.

Something that has to worry the rest of the league on top of the Spurs' well-chronicled new identity offensively and D that can still get into you (ask Kobe): How well will they be flowin' after the magical Rodeo Road Trip?

The Spurs, even with a two-game stumble in New York and Boston, were the first team in the league to win 30 games for the first time in franchise history. They're also the healthiest title contender going ... for a change.

How (else) do we know that the Spurs are rolling? They're shooting 77.7 percent from the free throw line, which happens to be the team's best reading from the stripe since 1979-80, when it shot 80.1 percent.

Without a 20-point scorer, San Antonio has 17 straight home wins and a 5 1/2-game lead on the rest of the West. That's the good news. The bad news? The Spurs finally have an injury worry: George Hill's right thumb.

If you're a Spurs fan who believes in omens, savor this while waiting for the next home game on Feb. 23: Six of the previous seven teams to win 40 games as fast as San Antonio just did went on to win the whole thing.

Normally I'd agree that the 50-game mark is too soon to be talking about magic numbers when it comes to clinching No. 1 in the West. These Spurs, though, have a seven-game cushion on their closest pursuers.

The Spurs ain't messin' around, even with that big lead over the rest of the West. How do we know? Pop responded to that one wack night in Philly with the first change to the starting lineup he's made all season.

The Spurs are a healthy six games up on the rest of the West after the Rodeo Road Trip, are still healthier than any contender and just watched another star leave the conference to go East. Must be an odd year.

We repeat: The Spurs are still a healthy six games up on the rest of the West, still healthier than any other contender and just watched another star (Melo) leave the conference to head East. Must be an odd year.

A 28-point halftime deficit to the Lakers after 22 home wins in a row was only the week's No. 2 surprise from the Spurs. Tony Parker coming back so quick was an even bigger shocker knowing their overly cautious ways.

The Suns shot 41.2 percent on 3s in 2009-10. Which is significant in San Antonio because that's the only team in the past 10 years with more team success from deep than these Spurs, who are hitting at 40.2 percent.

Tip your cap to the Spurs whether or not you think they've got enough size to get out of the West. This is their 15th season with at least 55 wins since merging into the NBA in 1976, second only to the Lakers' 19 in that span.

How bad are the Timmy (ankle) and Manu (thigh bruise) injuries? Serious enough, after a season of largely good health, to prompt rising panic in Alamo Country about holding onto the No. 1 seed, playoff prospects, etc.

Don't forget the worst stretch of the Duncan Era began with TD himself missing four of those six straight L's. Do we owe a retroactive apology to the West coaches slammed for making 34-year-old Timmy an All-Star?

Should the Spurs, holders of the league's best record since mid-November, lay down Tuesday night in L.A. to make sure the Lakers don't fall all the way to the No. 4 seed and right into their bracket? You tell me.

nop.summary: Don't think CP3 appreciated the suggestion in this cyberspace that he was still shaking off injury-related rust. Don't think we'll be repeating that suggestion, either, after the Hornets uncorked a Week 1 to rival anyone's.

The Hornets have never started 6-0 before. Ever. So you can safely assume that, yes, Chris Paul is pretty healthy and happy right now, despite our claim (laid out above) that No. 4 is as high as Team CP3 can go for now.

Fun factoid to keep the Hornets in Dreamland, even after they finally lose one: The last team to take an L in each of the past three seasons (Celts in '07-08, Lakers in '08-09 and Celtics in '09-10) all made it to the Finals.

Doubts about Jarrett Jack truly impacting CP's happiness are fair after we were all told upon Jack's arrival in Canada that he was super close with Bosh. But be advised also makes the league's hottest team better.

Apologies to the Hornets, who are 4-4 since that 8-0 start and bookended the week with a loss to the Clips and a fall-from-ahead L to the Spurs for their first home defeat. Looks as if the rankings' jinx still has some juice.

Severing ties with Shinn -- aka Donald Sterling of the South -- has to be a good thing in the grand scheme. Not that anyone in New Orleans is going to party amid a 2-6 skid and so much fresh uncertainty about the future.

Professor Hollinger summed up the Hornets' rising offensive woes with the sort of snark we had to steal: They scored fewer first-quarter points in Philly (13) than the Saints did (14) in their first quarter of American football.

If you were expecting more of a carryover in Detroit from the breakout rout CP3's Hornets laid upon D-Will's Jazz, you're not alone. At least we're seeing some Marcus Thornton again thanks to the Hornets' offensive woes.

They're not exactly back to their 11-1 form, but the wins over New Jersey and Atlanta were significant steps for the Hornets after the pain of their back-to-back road losses at Detroit (OT) and Indy (Dunleavy's tip at the buzzer).

Does a W in Boston, even when KG or Rondo are out, cancel out an L four nights earlier at 'Sota? Better question: Did you see how much harder Ariza made the Dunk of the Year race with that hammer over JaVale McGee?

So many targets (basically everyone apart from David West) are struggling offensively, so add an asterisk when citing the stat about the Hornets going 14-6 when CP3 has 10 or more dimes and 8-10 when he has less than 10.

Not many have noticed with so much Melo chaos unfolding and the usual focus on the big boys, but we have: New Orleans has won four in a row -- and five of six on the road -- in its first run resembling the 11-1 start.

Dare we say this 8-0 run -- achieved without the privilege of sneaking up on people -- is even more impressive than the Hornets' stunning 8-0 start. The similarities? Stifling D anchored by a very effective/engaged Okafor.

After a 10-game winning streak in which New Orleans held opponents to 86.8 ppg and became the only team in the league that to possess two wins over the Spurs, I suppose we can pardon one bad night in Sacramento.

Just as the recent 10-game win streak was actually more impressive than its 11-1 start, New Orleans' post-streak struggles are more worrisome this time. Way more thanks to the injuries to Okafor (oblique) and Ariza (ankle).

A 2-7 skid without the ailing Okafor to anchor the D, even after a 10-game winning streak, comes as zero surprise. Beating Dwight Howard's Magic without Okafor, in Orlando, for the second win in that span? Legit shocker.

The Hornets' roller-coaster season is clearly in one of those steep-dip cycles. They've lost six of seven without defensive anchor Okafor and CP3 really could have used a weekend off after dragging wearily into the break.

If you're missing your daily dose of superstar speculation that was a staple of the six months leading up to the trade deadline, fear not. You only have to wait until Wednesday night, when CP3 makes his solitary MSG stop.

Think I speak for just about all of us when I say it'd be great if we could rewind to, say, Wednesday. Back when the biggest concern about CP3 was that recent scoring dip as opposed to Sunday's scary stretcher scenes.

It was only the Kings, true, but give CP3 his post-concussion props: 33 points, 15 assists, seven boards and five steals in the same game has only been done by three others: Magic, Michael and, um, Nate Robinson!

Update from the Hornets' roller coaster: They shot out at 11-1, nosedived into a 7-13 funk, rose with a 13-2 rally, dipped again into a 4-12 rut and then went 5-2 before that fall-from-ahead loss at home to Boston.

The problem for the Hornets, even if they hang on to a playoff spot, is that they're going to see San Antonio without noted Spurs killer D-West ... or stay matched up with the Lakers. Which would probably be worse.

Like Karl and McMillan, Monty Williams is another guy who can't buy a COY mention. Quite a rookie season when you factor in the sale of the team to the NBA, D-West's season-ending knee injury and the constant CP3 chatter.

Props to CP3, Okafor and rookie coach Monty Williams (again): New Orleans' D has improved even more than Chicago's this season, down a league-leading 9.2 ppg ... compared to minus-7.8 ppg for Thibodeau's Bulls.

mem.summary: The stat, courtesy of ESPN.com's Tom Haberstroh, informs us that 16 of the last 17 teams to go unbeaten in the preseason -- as Memphis just did -- have gone on to reach the playoffs. Tantalizing stat if you're a Griz fan.

Some trivia for Griz fans to take in as they try (in vain) to forget the game their lads gave away in Phoenix: Rudy Gay just became the first player in franchise history to score at least 25 points in five consecutive games.

Thought we saw a breakthrough when the Griz won a one-point game in Dallas in the committee's presence. Yet each of the past two weekends featured painfully close L's in similar situations to Boston and at Phoenix.

Will not overreact to a home win over the Wade-less Heat because we already (foolishly) did that after their one-point W at Dallas. Gay is earning that money, but that's as far as it goes for Grizz proclamations here.

You can safely assume Mayo isn't thrilled with new sixth-man role, just as you can safely assume that the new job description will only increase outside trade interest in him. The Griz, though, are 3-1 since the switch.

Following up on the Phoenix comment: Who in the West's bottom seven is most likely to make us look bad in the next 3/4 of the season? Would still have to favor Portland or Houston, even with all their injuries.

They won in Dallas and beat both the Heat and Lakers at home, but you don't hear much about the Grizzlies' big nights. O.J. Mayo's future and owner Michael Heisley's playoff expectations are the big talking points. Still.

The best basketball from last season's Grizzlies came after Christmas and lasted through January. Just not sure they have the mojo or chemistry to do it again after what we will say has been a road-heavy December schedule.

What troubles you more, Grizz fans? The 1-13 record when allowing 100 points or more? Or the fact that the Grizz, Wolves and Bobcats are the only three teams that have never been asked to play on Christmas Day?

As if the Tyreke Evans heave from half court wasn't a sufficiently stunning way for the Grizz to lose one, be advised that those same Grizzlies just became the only team in the league this season to beat the champs twice.

That's a week the Grizz won't soon forget, after responding to the Tony Allen/O.J. Mayo scrap on the team's plane with three straight W's over winning teams (Lakers, Thunder, Jazz) for the first time since January 2004.

If the Grizz don't extend his contract before June 30, Z-Bo will be one of the most fascinating free agents of the eventual offseason. He's one of just five 20/10 guys going along with K-Love, Dwight, Blake and Boozer.

The only certainty, even when he's averaging 23.9 ppg and 14.3 rpg in January, is that Z-Bo has surpassed Gay as the Grizzlies' best All-Star hope. Can't promise anything more than that with all those forwards in the West.

Monday's date with Orlando is the only game in a stretch of 10 against a team with a winning record. The Grizz are mostly capitalizing on that stretch, too, starting off 5-1 despite the latest episode of Mayo Drama.

The Grizz wound up going 8-2 in that stretch of 10 games with only one foe possessing a record above .500. Not bad given what's going on with Mayo and compared to last season's second-half fade after a 25-19 start.

Is it possible that O.J. Mayo's 10-game suspension actually stabilized these guys? Hard to argue when the Grizz are 7-2 without Mayo, 14-5 when Sam Young is in the starting lineup and looking like real playoff material.

Since I've been as high on the Griz as anyone lately -- at least before Gay's shoulder matter -- I feel I can just be honest and admit it: In my head this week, I see Roddick's match-point dive for the ages when I hear Memphis.

Deepest Grizzlies team ever? That status was probably clinched even before last week, but Battier's return and the collapsed Mayo trade sealed the deal, which is why Rudy Gay's shoulder injury hasn't really hurt them yet.

Z-Bo generated very little All-Star snub pub, but the shot he rainbowed in to beat Dallas put the lefty and his Grizz in a rather exclusive club: No one else besides Memphis has three wins over the Mavs this season.

Down was the only way to go after wins over San Antonio and Dallas hiked the Grizzlies to No. 8 ... but they couldn't have crashed back to earth with a harder thud after Melo's buzzer-beater and the rout in Miami.

Worthy of the extension he's close to getting? Who would argue? Z-Bo was merely the first player in 42 years to be All-Star snubbed despite averaging 20 and 13; Nate Thurmond was the last ... at 23 ppg and 19 rpg in 1968-69.

One of the questions of the season: How are the Grizz -- now 10-6 against the West's top four and who just went 2-1 in a Boston/Chicago/San Antonio stretch with the first two on the road -- only a No. 8 seed?

Heisley demanded a playoff berth back in October. Now? Waiting to hear he expects a franchise that's never won a single playoff game to win a round ... which might not be so delusional depending on whom the Grizz draw.

Even after that costly home L to the Clips, I won't change my opinion: Memphis is the lower seed to fear most in the West even without Rudy Gay. The Spurs, Lakers and Mavs all dread seeing Z-Bo and Co. Trust me.

chi.summary: Who in Chicago is still willing to surrender Noah to Denver in a deal for Carmelo Anthony? Sixty mil over five years, even at a time when pretty much no one is scoring extensions, is looking like quite the bargain.

The Bulls' final home date before their annual circus road trip is Saturday's Derrick Rose-versus-John Wall track meet. Not the worst way to sign off before a hellacious seven-game jaunt. (Click here for the haunting details.)

Three straight W's and a winning record to take on their annual Circus Trip? With Boozer still injured and D-Rose forced to shoulder more of the scoring load than the Bulls would likely prefer? They'll take it. Gladly.

When Boozer comes back to join the long and rangy Noah and Gibson -- and especially if D-Rose starts getting to the line more than 5.5 times per game like he deserves -- these guys can challenge in the East. This season.

Not much more you have to say beyond running the final tab on the havoc D-Rose wreaked on the first winning Circus Trip (4-3) since MJ's last season running with the Bulls in 1997-98: 30.5 ppg, 6.5 apg and 5.7 rpg.

The Bulls are one of three teams with winning records, along with OKC and Phoenix, sporting a nightly point-differential margin of less than one. Not yet a cause for concern, though, when we've seen so little of Boozer.

The Bulls have 11 wins against Western Conference foes, and no other team in the East has more than six. D-Rose is shooting 41.6 percent on 3-pointers, and Boozer is back. Safe bet: Chicago is in the top 10 to stay.

This week's safe bet: Bulls fans are cursing us after we guaranteed -- in writing -- that their squad was in the top 10 to stay ... only for Noah, on cue, to go down with a long-term wrist injury. Of course we feel responsible.

If they had to lose Noah, this was the time. Four of Chicago's first five games without their chairman of the boards came against teams with losing records, as will nine of the next 10. Quite a gift for the holiday season.

Only Miami and San Antonio can top the Bulls' 13-2 record since Dec. 4. And we've barely seen Boozer and Noah together yet. And they still might upgrade at SG before the trade deadline. This team was not overhyped.

Losses to the Nets and Sixers were a shock to the system, even sans Noah, because the Bulls were 18-1 against sub-.500 teams going into those L's. But seeing D-Rose shred the KG-less Celts had to help Chicagoans rebound.

December began with L's to the Magic and Celts and forced thumb surgery on Joakim Noah halfway through the month, but D-Rose's Bulls are a tidy 18-5 since Dec. 4. Only the Spurs (19-3) and Heat (18-4) can top that.

You can probably guess the last time the Bulls were 30-game winners before the All-Star Game. In case you can't: Rewind to '97-98 for MJ's final Bulls season, when they started 34-15, finished 62-20 and three-peated.

Multiple ulcers for D-Rose. Only six games out of 47 with a full complement of big men. Yet somehow that adds up to a 25-6 record since Dec. 4, when a heavy loss to Orlando and an L in Boston left the Bulls at a humble 9-8.

Bulls fans miffed that they have only one All-Star should look at it this way: Even if East coaches only refused to pick Boozer because of how many games he missed, going to L.A. alone can't hurt D-Rose's MVP campaign.

Who in the East can be higher on the MVP ballot than D-Rose heading into the All-Star break? And, yes, I'd have posed the same question even before Rose's big games back-to-back on the road against D-Will and CP3.

This is the fifth-best team in Bulls history in terms of win percentage at the All-Star break ... and the other four had MJ. Factor in all the injuries and I don't quite get how D-Rose's MVP-worthiness can even be disputed.

Some reward we get for vaulting the Bulls above Boston to No. 3 last Monday. Hard to focus on Chicago's 8-5 record against the rest of the top six when it gives up 118, in Noah's first game back, to (yikes) Toronto.

No top-three team, East or West, had a more underwhelming road record than the Bulls' pedestrian 15-13 mark. Then they uncorked a weekend Florida sweep and really should have won in Atlanta to run the table.

If the Bulls somehow snag the East's No. 1 overall seed -- or just stay where they are and finish ahead of Miami -- please tell me what, exactly, would be wrong with voting Rose for MVP and Thibodeau for COY?

We repeat: If the Bulls manage to snag the No. 1 seed in the East -- or if they simply stay ahead of the Heat -- please tell us what, exactly, would be so wrong with voting Rose for MVP and Thibodeau for Coach of the Year.

Remember our recent suggestion in this cyberspace that the Bulls had to spruce up that pedestrian 15-13 road record? Check. They're 6-2 on the road since to help cement their status as the league's clear-cut No. 2.

Are the Bulls sitting in the top spot on this Monday morning if they don't lose last Monday night to Philly? Don't want to torture them too much, knowing how hard D-Rose takes this stuff, so we'll leave it at: Highly probable.

Every Bulls team that's ever won 60 games has gone on to win it all. So the least we can say about this one, however inexperienced, is that the sixth 60-win team in franchise history is the favorite in the East. Right?

uta.summary: Am I fearing that first face-to-face encounter with Jerry Sloan in case he's aware I dared to publicly engage in discussion about his Coach of the Year chances before a regular-season ball was dribbled? Yeah, kinda.

After that mighty struggle to take out the out-of-joint Clips -- who haven't won a game in Utah since January 2003 -- it's official: I definitely underestimated how much this Jazz misses how well Okur spaces the floor.

Everyone wants to talk about all the great escapes Utah just pulled off on its four-games-in-five-nights tour of the East. Me? Still thinking about the near loss to the Clips and how much it fueled this week of wild rallies.

Now that some of the shock and awe from Resurrection Week has worn off, do we dare suggest that continuously falling way behind A) isn't an advisable nightly strategy and B) hints at holes in D-Will's supporting cast?

Make that eight winning comebacks after facing a double-digit deficit in '10-11 before Sunday's rally versus the Clips ... although the repeated need for comebacks still strikes us as equal parts worrisome and awesome.

On top of all its double-digit comebacks, Team Living Dangerously is also 5-0 in games decided by six or fewer points. So maybe we were premature with the panic about Utah's ability to survive without Okur's floor spacing.

We say this not because D-Will (A) supplied our Mavs comment and (B) ranks as one of our faves ... but we can't shake the suspicion that the new Jazz are asking him to carry a load that's, well, a lot to carry for a full 82.

We repeat: Can't shake the suspicion that the reconfigured Jazz require D-Will to carry a nightly load that's realistically too much to shoulder for a full 82 games. Hope we're wrong, 'cause he's off to a career-year start.

They've lost every big game this month apart from a home date with the pre-trade Magic -- who were in full-on free fall at the time -- but the Jazz are bound to look back fondly on December now that Mehmet Okur is back.

You surely weren't surprised to see Utah sneak in one more double-digit comeback -- its 11th this season -- before the end of 2010 with Wednesday's road rally from 12 points down to beat the Clips. Were you?

Tough to get too revved up about Comeback No. 7 this season from 15 points or more down in Saturday's OT win over Houston -- even on the road -- when D-Will's Jazz are mired in a 10-8 malaise since their 15-5 start.

This is a different team -- a 20-1 team -- when it scores 100 points. With Okur back and C.J. Miles up to nine 20-point games off the bench, maybe Utah has a second half in store to render our OKC comment premature.

Disregard last week's mild optimism. The Jazz need to beat the Lakers in LA to avoid an 0-5 trip -- which began with L's to the Wiz and Nets -- and are hearing more frequent speculation (as predicted) about D-Will's future.

Remember all those second-half comebacks and the 15-5 start? The Jazz need a teamwide resurrection now after a 1-6 skid, with D-Will (wrist) ailing and Jefferson/Millsap not clicking any better than Jefferson/Love did.

While injuries are an undeniable factor in Utah's 3-9 slide, evidence continues to mount that D-Will will have to carry an unhealthy load during the stretch run just to ensure that the Jazz stays in the West's top eight.

It's not going to scare off suitors but it probably is a line worth filing away (as if D-Will, post-Sloan, wasn't already under the microscope): "I don't like being in the spotlight. It puts a lot of tension on me and I don't like it."

Jazz fans will surely be shellshocked at the next home game Monday night when Boston's in town, with neither Sloan nor D-Will in the building, but they have to applaud their team's proactivity. Absolutely have to.

It's honestly too soon to anoint trade deadline winners and losers. What if Melo and Amare are joined by a third star? Or if the Nets somehow get D-Will re-signed? But based on what we know now, Utah did as well as anyone.

Neither Sloan nor D-Will made it to the end of February. Only an OT win over the lowly Kings halted the first seven-game losing streak at home since 1982. All those comebacks early on? Cake compared to this.

This week's shock to the system for the reeling Jazz and their loyal fans: Friday night's heavy loss at Sota -- Sota! -- was Utah's seventh by more than 20 points, one shy of the league-high shared by the Wiz and Cavs.

With 12 games to go and a 5-10 record under Corbin and all but two of those games against top-eight teams in the West ... perhaps it's time to start getting used to the idea of the Jazz finishing the season under .500.

Overtime had been Utah's time all season until Thursday's crazy home L to New Orleans -- relive the prayer Okafor banked in at the regulation horn here -- dropped the crumbling Jazz (9-25 since a 27-13 start) to 5-1 in OT.

Chances are these are numbers Jazz fans are all too aware of by now, but for those of you not as up to speed since Sloan and D-Will left the scene: Elias says Utah is the first team ever to start 27-13 and miss the playoffs.

One last shock-to-the-system stat to cap a season of unprecedented upheaval in Utah: Corbin has that two-year contract extension ... but also has just six wins in 26 games with a team that's lost its fight post-Sloan.

mil.summary: Sorry, darlings. Top-10 status can be fleeting if you can't take care of Sota. And we've talked the Bucks up too much to let Friday's loss slide just because our guy Jennings responded with his first career triple-double.

Skiles, as always, has these guys overachieving on D. The issue has been the Bucks' O: They're last in the league in offensive efficiency after two weeks and thus pretty much headlining the list of early disappointments.

Are the Bucks "fixed?" It's premature to go that far, even after a tidy 3-0 week, but the numbers do tell us that Skiles somehow has them at No. 2 in defensive efficiency, allowing just 95.4 points every 100 possessions.

I want to believe, as an unabashed Bogut and Jennings fan, that the Bucks' offense is going to fix itself as Bogut's elbow gets stronger and Maggette and Salmons shake their recent ankle woes. Really, really want to.

Probably not hugely surprising given the Bucks' standing as the NBA's least efficient team offensively, but they've lost all three games decided by three points or fewer. (Miami and Philly are also 0-3 in one-possession games.)

Would have meant more, obviously, had Dwight Howard been playing. But Bogut didn't just return from injury Saturday night. That was last season's Bogut, rumbling for 31 and 18 and looking like the East's No. 2 center.

Life is goooood in the East. Cold but good. The Bucks' 7-13 start and various struggling signees (Gooden, Maggette, Salmons) add to undeniable disappointment ... but they couldn't drop lower than No. 8 if they tried.

Our fondness for Bogut and (the now injured) Jennings makes it hard to give in here, but Milwaukee just doesn't score enough to be a top-five team in the East. The most galling part: No. 5 is still so up for grabs.

Makes perfect sense that the Bucks, as inconsistent as they've been, manufacture a couple of road wins in Cali over the Lakers and Kings to tote into Christmas immediately after losing our man B-Jennings. Doesn't it?

Still like the Bucks better than any team outside the East's top four ... and still can't figure out if their schedule will ever ease up ... and still chuckle every Monday when I check to see if they've fallen out of the top eight yet.

Something tells me that the Bucks -- still waiting to see a full-strength Bogut alongside an unscathed Brandon Jennings -- ain't thrilled that their injured point guard has been lined up to participate in the dunk contest.

Of the Bucks' first 37 games, 26 came against .500-or-better teams. The combo of an easier schedule and health that has to get better is why you keep hearing know-it-alls like me say they have a second-half run in them.

Such are the depths of their woes on O that consecutive 100-point games against the Wizards and Cavs marked the battered Bucks' first back-to-back visits into triple digits since Nov. 9-10 against the Knicks and Hawks.

There was a time, don't forget, that the Bucks actually played in the West. In the East of today? Still see 'em as top-seven material now that Jennings and Delfino are back to go with a favorable second-half schedule.

The good news: Milwaukee hung in there at a passable 8-11 during a rough schedule patch while Brandon Jennings' broken foot healed. The bad news: Now our man Bogut has knee issues to go with that bad elbow.

The committee (of one) will be forced to concede at some point that the surge we've been promising from the banged-up Bucks ain't gonna happen. In the East, though, it's still too soon to make that concession.

Would love to claim that Redd's return can change everything. Well aware that only our stubborn devotion to lefties would lead us to claim that these Bucks have a 22-9 surge in store like they did after last season's break.

Charlotte's Gerald Wallace salary dump means Milwaukee is the only team outside the East's top eight that can even dare to dream of a late playoff push. But even we wouldn't dare claim that Redd's comeback fixes this team's ills.

More evidence to suggest that getting Bogut and Jennings healed is all that matters now: Milwaukee is 8-30 against teams at .500 or better. Only the Wolves (4-37), Wiz (7-33) and Cavs (8-33) are worse off.

Had a big speech planned about how the Bucks deserve the No. 8 spot more than Indy or Charlotte because they have the best chance of giving Boston or Chicago some semblance of a series. Then Sunday happened.

After a week to digest it and the Bucks' high-scoring weekend, I'm still trying to work out how they scored just 56 points in Boston ... one less than Redd's career-high and just one more than Jennings' 55 as a rookie.

Anyone worried that working Redd back into the flow might mess up chemistry at this critical juncture? If the Bucks couldn't handle Sacramento at home in the must-win portion of the season ... what chemistry?
After crushing L's in Charlotte and Indy, Milwaukee has the joy of becoming the 14th and final team to play a road back-to-back against the FLA teams

This will go down as the lowest-scoring team in Bucks history. But what hurts even more than all the injuries is knowing there's no Kareem in the draft to save them like the last Bucks team (1968-69) that shot it so poorly.

ind.summary: The first Monday of the regular season is a bit early to start talking about the MIP race, but Hibbert is forcing our hand. He's improved his passing as much as anything ... if you dare to judge after three games.

That's what we get for trying to launch into a MIP discussion in this cyberspace after three games. Certainly not putting it all on Hibbert, but the Pacers' two games since our last rankings were undeniably rough viewing.

You just had to know that the Pacers were going to follow up their third-quarter detonation against Denver by losing the next game by a point or three and wishing they didn't use up all that mojo in one night. Didn't you?

We continue with the premise that the Pacers used up too much mojo with those 144 points against Denver ... because the only time they've cracked 100 points in the five games since came against the defenseless Clippers.

Road wins over the Heat and Lakers? Sandwiched around a gut-wrenching OT loss to OKC? Throw in the recent narrow L to Orlando, and you get one the finest 3-2 stretches in the nine-season existence of this committee.

Losses at Utah and Phoenix won't discourage Indy deeply. Not after the Pacers began the trip with wins over the Lakers and Kings ... and with memories of an 0-8 mark on last season's two long West trips still fresh.
