Who had the Pacers finishing the first fourth of the season as a .500 team with D as their backbone and Hibbert emerging as a MIP threat with eight double-digit rebound games after just 10 total in '09-10? Not us, sadly.

No one's blaming Paul George, but facts is facts: Indy's tough schedule last week (Bulls, Lakers, Celtics) and resultant dip below .500 leaves Utah's Hayward and OKC's Aldrich as the only lottery picks on winning teams.

The idea that beating the Hornets on Dunleavy's buzzer tip would be some sort of turning point discounted the fact that they didn't play again for six days. The momentum-less Pacers then got pounded at home by the Grizz.

Remember November? Indy beat the Heat, then beat the Lakers in L.A. and generally reveled in Hibbert's darling status. Since then? The Pacers are 0-9 on the road and just watched Hibbert average 11 and 7 in December.

We were talking him up as an MIP contender in November, so Hibbert has to share a chunk of the culpability for the Pacers' slide since, which finds Indy in a 1-6 funk and Hibbert discussing his slump as candidly as you can.

Make that 0-4 when Indy goes for a third straight W. Detroit, Washington, New Jersey, Minnesota and Sacramento are the only other teams that have yet to win more than two in a row. (Notice Cleveland isn't on this list?)

Something tells me Pacer People, undoubtedly weary of hearing about those long-ago wins over the Heat and Lakers, got pretty giddy when they read about Larry Legend possibly hiring Kevin Pritchard for his front office.

Say this much for Larry Legend and the Pacers: They're giving little-known Frank Vogel every chance to get off to a good start as interim coach. Indy's first two games of the Vogel Era: Toronto at home, Cleveland away.

You have to factor in the soft schedule so far. Yet you also can't deny that the coaching change revived flatlining Indy, just as Silas' arrival did in Charlotte. Maybe we'll have a watchable race for No. 8 in the East after all.

So what if they've beaten only one team with a winning record (Portland) in this 7-1 start to the Frank Vogel era? In the season's first 44 games under O'Brien, Indy never managed to win three games in a row even once.

OK, OK: Maybe it's not the catchiest nickname. But Indy 100, if nothing else, is an appropriate capsule of the first 10 games of Vogel's tenure ... since the Pacers have cracked triple digits in every single one of them.

You like Indy's playoff chances more and more, even if Vogel's honeymoon is over, when you see Charlotte dumping salary and all the messed-up teams below. That tasty Mayo trade, though? Could have clinched things.

The collapsed Mayo trade still stings. Indy also just got swept in OKC, Dallas and Houston by 49 points combined. The consolation? Vogel is 4-5 on the road ... compared to a 1-14 road record in December and January.

Not so sure Hansbrough's clutch 29 points Sunday can pull Indy out of its costly recent funk. Yet we are sure that Durant, with 30 points in a Sonics uniform, is the only active player to score more in his MSG debut.

Retraction: Hansbrough is saving Indy's season with a March you can put up there with anything he did at North Carolina: 19.7 ppg and 7.7 rpg. Looks like Larry Legend was right. The kid should have been playin' all along.

The risk now is overhyping Hansbrough after the March he's had, but there's no disputing the fact that he crucially hatched his breakout right when the standard short-term spike from the coaching change had worn off.

It doesn't quite qualify as a late-season surge, but it's also not quite right to say Indy is completely backing into the East's eighth spot. The Pacers have bounced back from a double-digit deficit in four of their last five W's.

Even if he's a long shot to hang onto the job, Vogel is 20-17 since replacing Jim O'Brien, which means he can officially finish with a winning record no matter what his similarly inexperienced team does against the Bulls.

hou.summary: Have to go back to the 1999-2000 season for the last time Houston opened the season with three successive losses. Doesn't seem possible with the sort of domination Scola has carried over from the Worlds in Turkey.

The five teams (Lakers, Warriors, Nuggets, Hornets and Spurs) that ushered the Rockets to an 0-5 start are a combined 25-5. That's the good news. The really bad news: PG Brooks (ankle) just went down for four to six weeks.

The Rockets are as optimistic as they can be after a 1-6 start and with Yao's comeback interrupted by a fresh ankle injury. Reason being: They've held a lead in the fourth quarter in all but one game so far.

Still no Yao. No Aaron Brooks. No wins in seven tries when the Rockets allow 100 points. And virtually no defense to speak of in the two games since since the heartbreak of a narrow home loss to Chicago.

Durant's buzzer miss Sunday might've been Houston's first fortuitous bounce of the season. The Yao/Aaron Brooks-less Rockets took a perfectly blemished record of 0-7 when held under 100 points into that game.

The weight of carrying the offense was wearing on Scola and Kevin Martin, who aren't being smothered quite as resolutely by opposing defenses now that Lowry and Brad Miller have returned to shoulder some of the load.

It's obviously not going to get you noticed in a league with those aforementioned four teams having won at least eight in a row. The Rockets, though, are creeping back toward normalcy at 9-9 since their 0-5 start.

You figured the Rockets, deep down, were expecting the devastatingly bad news about Yao's potentially career-ending setback. Not the vibe we're getting, though. They really did think he'd be back sometime this season.

All-Star long shots with sick stats? Make room in your club, Kevin Love and Monta Ellis, for Kevin Martin, whom Elias says is on pace to become the first player to lead the league in total FTs and 3s made in a season. Ever.

Some of their turnaround is schedule-related, but it's happened before with the Rockets and happened again this season: They do tend to play better once they know for sure Yao isn't coming back. Cruel as it sounds.

The reward for scraping all the way back to .500 after that 0-5 start? Nine games out of 10 against teams with winning records ... with Houston off to an 0-5 start in 2011 and four more toughies on this week's schedule.

Road wins of the highest quality, in Boston and Atlanta, only somewhat ease the Rockets' dismay with themselves, after falling to 0-4 in overtime games and a recent four-game skid in which they led by at least nine in all four.

Isn't Kevin Martin the ultimate All-Star snubee? Daily debates rage on about the obstacles Blake, K-Love and Monta face to make the West roster. For all his offensive efficiency, Martin doesn't even get those mentions.

The standings say Houston still has some measure of hope for sneaking into a West playoff spot. The Rockets' 12-18 record against their conference rivals -- 2-9 since the calendar flipped to 2011 -- says otherwise.

The good news? Houston finally won a game in OT on the sixth try and had to beat the scorching Grizz to do so. The bad news? No more Grizz games left this season, with Kev Martin averaging 31.3 points against them.

Walking off the floor with time still left on the clock is about as far away from MIP standards as Aaron Brooks could have strayed, but the Rockets insist they won't surrender Brooks in a trade unless it's part of a megadeal.

The Rockets dreamed of being the team that found a way to concoct a trade for Melo. They had to settle for the very unsatisfying consolation prize of sending Melo to his final loss as a Nugget. On Valentine's Day.

We'll get back to the Kev Martin show and Scola's injury scare soon enough. In the meantime ... telephone call for Hakeem Olajuwon. The big man who needs your tutoring more than any other -- Thabeet -- is now a Rocket.

With Kevin Martin clicking, their D tightening and a home-heavy schedule? You have to like the Rockets' chances of cracking the top eight better than fading Utah's, even if they still haven't spent a day over .500 yet.

If the Rockets ultimately miss the playoffs, as seems likely now, here's one key culprit: They have nine losses after leading in the final three minutes of the fourth quarter or OT, behind only Detroit and Minnesota (10).

These are the days that longtime Rockets fans, remembering how their team actually used to play out of the East, see them stuck at No. 9 after winning 11 of 14 and must wonder what it would take to switch back.

What does the league's No. 3 record (12-4) since the All-Star break get you? In the Rockets' case, it likely still leaves them needing an 8-1 finish and a Hornets fold after losing D-West just to get into the tournament.

They're on pace to finish with a better record than three East playoff teams. They're the NBA's No. 4 team since the All-Star break at 15-5. And they're on fumes, playoff-wise, because the West-less Hornets refuse to crumble.

They started the season 0-5 and started 2011 with five straight L's, too. Two rough stretches that helped keep a game, hot Houston team (along with last week's painful L's to the Kings and Hornets) out of the playoffs.

phx.summary: After routinely getting pummeled in the exhibition season and flaming out in the fourth quarter in Portland on opening night, these guys are starting to look a little bit more like the Suns. Two straight games in the 100s.

You thought the way Phoenix forced overtime in Friday's win over Memphis was wild? Get this: You have to go back to 1999-2000 for the last time Nash began a season with five straight games with fewer than 10 assists.

The Suns obviously aren't going to drill 22 triples every night like they just did in Lakerland. Yet they've clearly got some grit left over from last season judging by how they've coped with this brutal early schedule.

Losing Lopez made a tiny team painfully smaller. Losing Nash next made watching lil' Phoenix painful, as evidenced by the Saturday night surrender of 123 points to a Charlotte team that never scores like that.

You don't have to have your own rankings formula like Professor Hollinger to know that allowing 138 points to the Nuggets -- when Melo plays only two minutes -- sounds about as good to Alvin Gentry as trading Nash.

I will pretend later that I never even suggested this if the statement proves to be ridiculously premature, but are the top eight we see in the West right now -- with Phoenix at No. 8 -- the same eight bound for the playoffs?

Our guy Nash hasn't played on a sub-.500 team since the 40-42 Mavs in '99-00. Don't think his Suns will sink that far, but expecting better  than a No. 8 seed is folly given the Suns' size/depth/defensive shortcomings.

Nash to our man Paul Coro of the Arizona Republic: "I know a lot of people are telling me to demand a trade. If I demand one, does that mean I get to pick my team? No. It's not that simple. ... I signed here to play here ..."

One thing that hasn't changed amid all the new faces and probably won't no matter who the Suns put around Steve Nash: They've got to get to 100 points to have a chance to win. When they don't? It's an 0-9 team.

The bad news? Loss No. 5 in six games was sealed by giving up 19 of the final 21 points in an epic collapse at lowly Sactown. Worse news? Amare makes his return to Phoenix on Friday night. Somewhat triumphantly, too.
Not sure which was worse. Getting smoked LeBron-returns-to-Cleveland-

The recent home escape against a Cavs team starting Manny Harris and Christian Eyenga began a stretch with seven games out of 10 against sub-.500 teams. A stretch Alvin Gentry openly admits "is basically our season."

Guest comment straight out of Ric Bucher's chat: "These [recent] wins are putting lipstick on a pig. There is no quick fix for the Suns, other than trading Nash and accepting that you're tearing this down to the studs."

Not getting picked by the West coaches in 2009 -- when the game was in Phoenix -- had to sting. Something tells me Nash won't mind a snub much this time if the Gortat we saw over the weekend keeps showing up.

Now that the coaches and their commissioner have found a way to make room for Duncan, Blake and Love on the West's All-Star roster, can we all agree that Nash is the biggest West snub ahead of Aldridge and Z-Bo?

This wasn't a mere bad L at home. Sunday night saw the Suns lose to the Cousins-less Kings only after nudging past .500 for the first time since Dec. 7 (11-10) and having held three consecutive foes under 100 points.

See Nash's line about how he snubbed the All-Star Game? Channing Frye, meanwhile, didn't even want an All-Star break; 55 points against Dallas and Utah last week marked the biggest two-game outburst of Frye's career.

Two straight Mondays in this space for Channing Frye? He left us no alternative with that buzzer-beater for the win in Indy, which was the Suns' first since a game-winner from Quentin Richardson in December 2004.

Sunday's events were undeniably painful. Especially for Vince Carter. But an OT loss at OKC, even combined with Dallas' inability to hold a 17-point lead over Memphis, can't undo the overall goodness of a 4-2 road trip.

Ten comebacks this season from 10 points or more down. Six wins at home when trailing after three quarters. And all talk about the Suns' rallying powers/playoff chances is hereby moot if Nash can't heal. Quickly.

Although it appears he has survived his bout with "pelvic instability," our guy Nash clearly wasn't quite in top gear in New Orleans in the first of the Suns' three remaining must-win games against the Hornets.

Nash has quietly wrested the assist lead away from Rondo, but I grudgingly have to concede that the best efforts of Captain Canada, Grant Hill and the best sixth man no one talks about -- Marcin Gortat -- won't be enough.

It's safe to say Nash needed a break, flu or not. He's clearly been operating at less than 100 percent in a vain attempt to drag the Suns into the playoffs, as his decline from 16.8 ppg to 10.9 ppg since the All-Star break suggests.

The irony in the desert, if we can leap to the conclusion that Nash (37) and Grant Hill (38) aren't going to be there forever, is that it looks as if the center spot (Gortat) is the only position they're set going forward.

gsw.summary: The sale of the team isn't quite complete and Curry is already nursing an ankle issue, but the Dubs are also still basking in the glow of the biggest opening night eruption -- Monta's 46 -- since MJ went for 54 in 1989.

The Dubs haven't started like this at home (4-0) since Run TMC opened 6-0 in Oaktown way back in 1990-91. So they don't really care that two of the victims (Rockets and Griz) were on the back end of a back-to-back.

The Dubs have lost D-Lee for at least a week in a fairly freaky incident. So we can only conclude -- after a 6-2 start, glimpses of Curry/Ellis cohesion and Dorell Wright's sudden improvement -- things were going too well.

You keep reading and hearing about how soft the early schedule has been, as if the Dubs are going to apologize. After the Cohan Era -- one playoff trip in the past 17 seasons -- 5-1 at home feels unapologetically spectacular.

Surprising: Golden State is a heady 7-1 with D-Lee in uniform (1-8 without him). Stunning: Heat castoff Dorell Wright is tied with Jason Richardson for the league lead in most games with at least six 3-pointers (three).

Here's why long-suffering Golden State wouldn't apologize about how cushy its early schedule was: After Spurs/Suns/Thunder last week, its next four opponents are Mavs/Spurs/Heat/Jazz. With only Miami at home.

The Dubs want to believe their season starts for real after a run of seven straight tough assignments ends Monday night in Utah. But what really hurt, obviously, was losing D-Lee when the schedule was cushy early.

Is a Christmas Day audience really ready for the Dubs? Better question: Is a Christmas Day audience, even in the late-late-late game, really ready for the graphic shots we're sure to see of that gnarly hole in David Lee's elbow?

The Dubs, remember, haven't had an All-Star since Spree in '97, but the skeptic in me still says Monta's recent eruptions (44, 36 and 39 points) in his best-ever season can't halt that drought. Not in the guard-heavy West.

The focus is naturally on the 20-point lead they blew in Miami. The closest thing to consolation is the fact the Dubs won by a point the night before in Charlotte ... only their second one-point W in the past four seasons.

No team has played more road games than Golden State's 22. And the Dubs -- as healthy as they've been in ages -- have 17 of the next 20 games at home. Doubt that'll spark another "We Believe" campaign, but it's a start.

The Warriors' first stop after this crazy stretch of home games (16 of the next 19) is Feb. 27 in Minnesota. Our question: Will Monta Ellis and K-Love be reliving All-Star glories or commiserating about their snubs?

The Dubs' first four-game win streak since 2008 and two Monta daggers -- a game-winning pull-up J against Indy, then a game-tying 16-footer against Sacramento -- had to help his All-Star campaign. Or at least couldn't hurt.

AOL's Chris Tomasson just reminded us that one of our absolute high school faves -- Purvis Short -- averaged 28.0 ppg for the Dubs in '84-85 and got an All-Star snub ... just so Monta Ellis knows that he wouldn't be the first.

Doesn't matter that all three victims were missing All-Star-caliber talent (D-Will, Bogut and Noah). When the Dubs hold three straight teams under a hundred, there can be no other topic worthy of the comment space.

Good luck convincing OKC that the Dubs' Ellis-and-Curry backcourt is too small to survive. The defensively challenged duo combined for 56 points and 20 assists against just four TOs in Sunday's win over the Thunder.

No one out West has more road games left, but the Dubs also have 10 more wins than they did at this point last season, which trails only San Antonio (14), New Jersey (12) and Miami (12). In other words? They'll take it.

Rough week. The Dubs thought they were getting Antawn Jamison on deadline day, couldn't quite reach terms with Cleveland, then began a season-defining stretch (12 out of 15 on the road) with a loss at Sota.

To have any playoff shot? Five games into that season-defining stretch (12-of-15 on the road), it's already clear (after four narrow L's) that the Dubs had to do better than 12-10 when they had 18-of-22 at home.

Makes total sense. The Dubs couldn't win in Sota, Indy or Jersey on a road trip that had to go well to preserve any playoff hope ... then back home they find a way to corral Dwight Howard and Kevin Love back-to-back.

Love and Aldridge might be the MIP favorites, but Dorell Wright has to be in the conversation. Did you catch how much he improved Friday night in Phoenix? Zero points at halftime ... followed by 30 points after the break.

Road woes extinguished whatever playoff fantasies Golden State had, and here's at least one source of its travel trouble: Monta averages 27.8 ppg at home and 20.8 ppg on the road. It's the league's largest discrepancy.

No one's suggesting it's all his fault, but Smart's odds of returning as coach seem slim, because the Dubs have just seven more W's than last season, improved marginally on D and sport the West's third-worst road record.

Instead of reveling in their hard-to-fathom sweep of the Mavs, Blazers and Lakers that certainly couldn't have hurt Keith Smart's job security, they've been reduced to the Worriers again after iron man Monta's scary fall.

sac.summary: The Kings overturned a 16-point deficit Saturday night in Cleveland to move to 2-1. Casspi scored 20 and drained six triples in the win, four in the second half. Surely you weren't expecting an Omri-free comment.

The Kings' brief rise into the top 20 was surely dismissed in some precincts as a byproduct of Omri-related exuberance. Yet we still say going 3-1 with three games on the road, for this unproven crew, made it a legit bump.

Tension/frustration has mounted so quickly in the wake of that 3-1 start -- with the help of a hugely favorable schedule, it must be said -- that Tyreke's bid for another 20/5/5 season has barely been mentioned lately.

Enraged as I am to see my man Casspi take the heat for some collectively woeful D to date, there's not much I can say when the Kings hold the Nets and Hornets to 81 and 75 points in the first two games post-lineup change.

Cousins, like the Knicks' Fields, is also on the four-man short list of rookies scoring in double figures along with Griffin and Wall. The defenseless Kings, though, can't enjoy it amid all the losing and Tyreke's soph slump.

Remember how fun and scrappy they were with last season's 13-14 start? Now chew on this: The Kings are 15-55 since Geoff Petrie's contract extension was announced in December 2009 when they were at 14-16.

The Kings' pain is bound to continue with Tuesday's visit to Houston, where they'll find Kev Martin fresh off his first 40-point game as a Rocket and scoring with All-Star-ish efficiency ... while Landry sits on the trade block.

The Kings always will be relevant to the committee (of one) as long as they employ that Casspi kid. But it's got to be torture for the Maloofs for their team, given its early 2000s glory, to matter so little in the grand scheme.

Kings co-owner Joe Maloof insists both Westphal and Petrie will survive the season. Yet it says here, if you're keeping score, that the GM is in greater peril than the coach thanks to a 17-65 nosedive since last season's 13-14 start.

Tyreke celebrated that buzzer-beater like a guy well aware that the Kings have had the easiest schedule in the league so far based on opponent winning percentage ... which is to say things are only bound to get tougher.

The last couple of weeks have clued us all in on the fuss surrounding Cousins and why, no matter how much trouble he gets in, Sacramento has deemed him untouchable: 21.9 ppg and 9.2 rpg over the last six games.

If the Kings trade Beno Udrih, it's to shed his contract more than anything. Hard to blame the Slovenian for much when, in support of the blossoming Cousins, he's averaged 20.8 points in Sacramento's past six games.

The Kings followed their big win at MSG with four straight narrow defeats, including the last two in OT. The solace: January Tyreke (19.4 ppg, 6.7 apg, 44.4 percent shooting) finally looks a little more like ROY Tyreke.

Team of the Week? There's no other choice after the Kings' Cousins-powered weekend wins over the Lakers and Hornets. A rook hadn't rumbled for 27 points and 10 rebounds on L.A.'s floor since Christian Laettner ... in March 1993.

Three games left in a seven-game run in which every opponent is above .500. Then the Kings' kids play their next seven games on the road, stopping in Phoenix, OKC, Dallas, Miami, Orlando, Charlotte and Memphis. Yikes.

Question: Why do the Kings put up with their marquee rookie's perpetual volatility? Answer: Cousins averaged 17 points and 8 boards in January and is averaging 17 and 11 in February against very strong opposition.

The only deadline that matters in Sactown, whether or not a trade is in store, is seven days away. That's the March 1 buzzer for the Kings to apply for relocation to Anaheim if they want to move in time for next season.

Arco Arena will be full Monday night when the locals try to sway the Maloof brothers sitting courtside and rally support for keeping the Kings. It's the rare occasion that having Blake Griffin in town is actually secondary.

He only just got there, but maybe no one would miss Sacramento more than Marcus Thornton. With Tyreke out, it's been a veritable green-light district for the newest King (21.2 ppg so far) to launch and launch.

Looks like 18 games left for No. 18 as a Sacramento King ... with only eight of them actually in Sacramento. (This, incidentally, is the first Casspi reference in this comment space for full 12 weeks. Restraint!)

Not the most fitting farewell to a building that used to be the noisiest around: Sacramento is the only team out West with fewer than 10 home wins ... with (likely) only five games left at once-feared Arco Arena.

They're not just playoff spoilers. Back-to-back-to-back wins in Milwaukee, Indy and Philly got the Kings in the same sentence with Dallas ... since they're the only two teams better on the road than they are at home.

It would actually capture the theme of this ominous season pretty well, come to think of it, if the Kings go to Anaheim as the NBA's only team with a better record on the road than at home. Which is where they are now.

Two more home games left for the Cousins/Evans/Thornton trio to improve on the recent 7-4 surge and pad the franchise record of 540-384 at Arco Arena before the inevitable move to the committee's home turf in OC.

bkn.summary: They got trounced at home by the Heat, true. But let's let the Nets enjoy the moment for a minute: They're just the fourth team in history to open a season 2-0 after winning fewer than 20 games in the previous season.

Think we all knew 2-0 was a mirage for Avery's kids when they had to play Miami twice and Orlando within their next four. But even the biggest Nets cynic surely never expected Lopez to shoot 14-for-50 in three games.

Even if poor ball movement and a lack of scoring threats around Brook Lopez were the prime causes for his recent 21-for-73 shooting slump, as his coach believes, getting Lopez right ASAP is Job 1 for Jersey at the minute.

Progress report? Five straight Ls in games decided by five points or fewer, one public plea already from the new coach for more toughness and accountability and zero double-doubles for a presumed All-Star in Lopez.

If the rumors are true about Kris "Career Year" Humphries and Kim Kardashian, maybe Prokhorov wins that ring sooner than anyone thinks, as the Saints (Kim, Reggie Bush) and Lakers (Khloe and Lamar) could tell you.

After the week the Nets just endured -- heavy L's to the hated Knicks and Celts sandwiched around two OT defeats and more Lopez inconsistency -- they surely wish we'd kept the focus on Humphries and Kardashian.

Avery Johnson never lost more than four straight games as the Mavs' head coach. Latest reminder he's not in Dallas anymore: New Jersey has dropped seven in a row to plummet to the foot of the Eastern Conference.

Is it as simple as Devin Harris scoring 21 points or more? Hard to argue when these numbers arrive from the ESPN Stats & Info folks: New Jersey is 7-1 when Harris scores at least 21 ... and 1-19 when he doesn't.

Nine wins by Christmas doesn't sound so bad when you remember last season's Nets didn't get that many until March 26. Nothing's changed, though. Hard to think of anything else in Jersey beyond the Melo Sweepstakes.

Elias somehow found a stat that might make the Nets feel a hair better about themselves: New Jersey's three Ls by 15 points or more since Dec. 21 don't lead the league in that span. Not when the Lakers (wow) have four.

It's not something that compares to anything happening on the Melo front, but having 10 wins at this stage is a moderately sized deal for a team that (A) is in Melo limbo and (B) didn't win that many last season until March 29.

The Brook Lopez whom the Nets can excitedly sell to Melo: 35 points and 32 points in his past two games. The Brook Lopez whom the Nets hope Melo hasn't heard about: Only two double-digit rebound games all season.

Can't even pretend to claim this is any sort of consolation prize, but it is a fact: New Jersey played its best ball of the season -- with wins over Utah and Detroit and a one-point L to Dallas -- after pulling out of the Melo talks.

Nuggets at Nets on Monday night. Melo's lone scheduled appearance of the season at Prudential Center. Sources say that a bigger crowd is expected postgame in Melo's locker room than for the actual game.

Have to point out -- after years of hassling Devin Harris about his QB-ing -- that he's posted games with 16, 18 and 13 dimes in his past five outings. It's, well, something to talk about apart from Melo disappointment.

Saturday night marked the first time in NBA history that road teams went 8-for-8 in a single day. Yet I assure you no home team was more bummed than the Nets, who couldn't take down the Amare-less Knicks.

When the Nets made their back-to-back Finals trips, they were led by a franchise guy with a long-term contract. After last summer's strikeouts and the Melo tease, Prokhorov needs to find a trade for his own Jason Kidd.

The Nets know. They know there's a long way to go before D-Will warms to the idea of Brooklyn. Yet as risky as the deal was, given the assets surrendered for a guy who can leave in 16 months, they couldn't say no.

Two overseas wins over the Raps aren't going to net much global recognition, but Prokhorov and Co. did see the Brook Lopez of their dreams in London: 32 points, 14 boards and eight blocks in triple OT.

Kris Humphries' life-changing season continued against Blake Griffin's Clips: Elias says he's just the third player ever to shoot 8-for-8 (or better) and snag 20 boards ... next to Wilt (nine times) and Dikembe (once).

Another entry for Kris Humphries' life-changing season: 15 or more boards in every game of the Nets' recent five-game win streak is a feat only one other active player has matched: KG with 'Sota way back in 2004-05.

Relieved to hear that D-Will is going to try to test that bad wrist this week. A third straight week with an entry from Kris Humphries' life-changing season -- he's at 14.1 rpg since the All-Star break -- is pushing it.

Can't resist a fourth successive Kardashian-related comment. And not just because we like writing about her. Even Hump himself is publicly crediting the Kim K. Factor as at least partial justification for the best ball of his life.

Prokhorov got his star in the end, but the finish to his first full season in charge -- losing game after game to sweeten Utah's pick with D-Will and Hump sidelined -- is almost as torturous as the months spent chasing Melo.

cle.summary: Who had the LeBron-less Cavs winning every exhibition except the CSKA Moscow game ... then beating Boston in their opener after the Celts had beaten Miami ... and then losing to the Raps and Kings? Right: Not you.

Totally guilty of stealing this line from Adande, but can't resist -- This morning's standings supply the best  if the playoffs started today setup of all time: No. 4 Cleveland would open against No. 5 Miami in Round 1.

The post-LBJ Cavs have already seen some happier days than many of us envisioned, with three straight road Ws in addition to the big Boston win. Yet they've also lost four in a row at home for the first time since March '03.

The Cavs took a .500 record into back-to-back games on the road against the top two teams on our list. So, yes, there are roughly 10 to 20 people in Cleveland who feel borderline good about NBA basketball these days.

Think back to July -- or even October -- and tell me you would have dared to predict that the jilted Cavs would be starting the week of LeBron's return to the Q with the East's eighth seed and only two fewer W's than Miami?

A 34-point beatdown in Minnesota after the total laydown in LeBron's return in Cleveland with the world watching? The worst week in franchise history was unquestionably July 5-11, 2010 ... but you just witnessed No. 2.

Does the fact that Izzo is (allegedly) fed up with his Michigan State players after turning down the Cavs' job bring any solace to Cavs fans? Didn't think so. Impossible after eight straight L's by a combined total of 160 points.

How badly did the Cavs need that OT escape against the Knicks? Losing the night before at Indy had just made them the first team EVER to endure a double-digit skid after winning 60 or more games in the previous season.

The nightmare collapse that began with a home L to Boston in the game before LeBron's homecoming just reached 1-13  thanks to a home L inflicted by a team (Minnesota) that LeBron just nominated for contraction.

Time for B-Scott to dig out all those preseason picks again that made the Cavs so mad and allegedly fueled their 7-9 start. They went 1-14 in Dec. and got outscored by 13 a game ... compared to Miami's 15-1 month.

I swear the goal isn't to measure the Cavs against LeBron's Heatles every week. This week, though, it's tough to resist the symmetry with the Cavs in a 1-20 funk, down to just that one win in the last 43 days. To be precise.

At least there's still faint hope here of returning to the lofty heights of No. 29 with a hard-to-envision win streak at some stage. In Hollinger's system? Not sure you can recover from consecutive losses of 55, 22 and 28.

Something tells me you won't be surprised to hear that the Cavs -- with one win in 54 days now -- are on course to become the first team in history to go from the league's-best record to the worst record in one season.

Denver in '97-98. Vancouver in '95-96. Dallas in '93-94. And Philly, of course, in '72-73. Those were the only four teams in history that knew how it felt to lose 20 in a row ... before these post-LeBron Cavs joined the club.

It won't quite crack this Sunday's ABC lineup with Miami in Boston and the Lakers going to Orlando, but isn't Wiz at Cavs your game of the week? You must have the Cavs winning a game between now and then if not.

Now that The Streak is over, we go directly to Ohioans for a ruling: Do you put 26 straight L's with an injury-shredded, post-LeBron roster down there in the two-word pantheon with The Drive, The Fumble and The Betrayal?

Now you know why Hollinger calls these the "human" rankings. The professor's heartless computer will never forget a 55-point loss or 26 L's in a row. Us? Just could not keep the Cavs at No. 30 after what they did to L.A.

On your list of players to grieve for, Jamison has to be up there. So close to a trade back to Golden State on deadline day, Jamison didn't get the reprieve Mo Williams got. What he got was a fractured finger three nights later.

Hickson's been quietly figuring things out over the past month, Baron as a Cav is must-see and April 3 must be circled on your calendar with Cleveland going for a 4-0 sweep of the Knicks that night at MSG. No joke.

It's been that kind of season: Just getting newcomers Semih Erden and Luke Harangody on the floor to help the Cavs make it through the dog days of the schedule has been an ordeal thanks to injury obstacles.

It's down to the Nets and the Cavs. Those are the only two teams in the league without a 20-point victory this season after the Mavs -- what took so long? -- finally got their rout Sunday night by drubbing the Dubs.

There haven't been many happy Mondays for Cavs fans. So let's focus this one on Sunday night's uplifting return of iconic radio broadcaster Joe Tait as opposed to LeBron's second visit to the Q coming Tuesday night.

A season sweep of NY would have been sweet, but you won't hear any complaining out of Cleveland. Not after the Cavs followed up the emotional return of Joe Tait by giving the team's radio legend a W over LeBron to call.

Some big wins for a team that will be remembered for a record 26-game losing streak: Boston in the opener. The Lakers right before the All-Star break. And Miami in March to avenge LeBron's triumphant first game back.

nyk.summary: First impressions from the committee's rare MSG visit Saturday night: Amare has changed the atmosphere there. He's given the Knicks legitimacy after years without it. Not nearly enough around him, though. Not yet.

The weekend provided a telling illustration of life around the Knicks: Way too much was made of the big W in Chicago, and too much panic is bubbling anew after Sunday's home L to Philly halted a two-game win streak.

Maybe it's too soon to start making Titanic Division cracks. Or maybe not when the Celts already have a 4 1/2-game lead on their closest pursuer (Nets) and the Knicks (with five straight L's) looking fragile and fractious.

The committee was holed up in Gotham when a two-game winning streak inflated Knicks expectations. Can only imagine how unrealistic some folks will be now after three straight road wins over some West lottery teams.

The Knicks' victims in this 6-1 run have a combined record of just 44-75. But five of those wins came on the road ... and Landry Fields is one of only four rookies averaging double figures. Let Spike Lee enjoy the moment.

Love the way, as usual, that our man Hojo Beck wrote it in the NYT: The caveat to the caveat -- how Knicks foes have the league's lowest combined winning percentage at .415 -- is the fact the Knicks are 9-4 on the road.

I know, I know. The combined record of the eight teams felled during the Knicks' win streak is 71-118. But it can't be all about opposition quality when a team wins 13 of 14 and eight of those W's come on the road.

Did we overstate the Knicks' 13-2 run before their 0-3 plummet to Earth? We and everybody else. As my man Scott Howard-Cooper of NBA.com suggests, maybe we did need to focus more on the 13 teams they beat.

The Knicks might have impressed us more with the bounce-back wins over the Thunder and Bulls -- remembering what happened against Boston, Miami and Cleveland -- than they did with the 13-1 run against patsies.

Have they fluttered back to Earth after that 13-2 joyride? Sure. Did the Knicks pass around a copy of the standings at practice to fully soak in the six-game cushion they've already got on No. 9 Philly? Presumably.

Don't mind the hate tweets from Knicks fans 'cause their squad has been down for so long. Let 'em enjoy the moment. Wins over the Spurs and Suns, furthermore, suggest maybe I did have 'em too low last time. Maybe.

You know by now that I'm going to mention Bernard King every chance I get, so thanks, Amare: Stoudemire's 24 straight games with at least 20 points tied BK for third in team history, five behind Richie Guerin's record.

You're seeing now why Amare edged D-Rose for East MVP of the first trimester. Rose is bound to be in the MVP race to the finish, but we had to make sure Amare got his props before the Knicks, as feared, took a tumble.

Timely as it was to reel off three successive home wins after that six-game skid, there's comfort for the Knicks whenever they look at the East standings, where they see no one below them even close to the .500 Club.

The NBA's single-game scoring record on the day of the Super Bowl is Pistol Pete's 50-point game in 1972. In his 50th game as a Knick, Amare made a nice run for it in Sunday's win over Philly with a forceful burst of 41.

It's one thing to be distracted by trade speculation. It's quite another to publicly complain about it as much as the Knicks have. Equally disturbing: New York is a mere 14-25 when you throw out that magical 13-1 stretch.

The wait is over! The Knicks had a winning record at the break for the first time since 2000-01. The other wait's over, too. Breaking up a team barely holding off Philly for the No. 6 seed to lock up Melo now? Had to do it.

The East's best will surely put a lot more stock into what they saw from the new Knicks in Miami than what they showed us in Cleveland. Trust us: No top-four seed wants to see Amare and Melo in a first-round series.

Make all the jokes you want about how the Knicks are praying they don't see Cleveland in the first round. They've still got two elite scorers none of the big boys want to see to go with Melo's two losses to the Cavs.

Are the Knicks trying for Miami in the first round as opposed to trying to swipe Atlanta's No. 5 seed? That's how it looks when they follow up two losses to the Cavs with Melo with a home loss to floundering Indy.

Five losses in six games, unsavory Melo headlines everywhere and Delfino just became the fourth player this season (joining Hansbrough, Love and Griffin) to bag his first career 30-point game against the Knicks. Ouch.

Ouch continued: Melo is chafing under the spotlight he thought would be "easy" to handle, Amare looks drained and confused trying to learn how to play alongside him and Chauncey is both ailing and a questionable fit.

You know we don't waste chances to reference Bernard King. Kudos, then, go to Melo -- despite all the recent angst and criticism -- for being the first Knick since my King in 1984 to ring up three straight 35-point games.

Guess who just posted their first winning season since going 48-34 in 2000-01 and -- after the national pounding Melo took for that recent 1-9 swoon -- has quietly matched the league's longest active win streak held by Chicago?

was.summary: Early contender for upset of the season: An editor (Justin Verrier) made an Oasis reference to John "Wonder" Wall (scroll down the right side of the Weekend Dime to see his headline) before I could. Clearly slipping.

Is there a sub-.500 team you'd rather watch than the Wiz? Especially now that Gil is back? We say no even after two weekend L's that snuffed out the euphoria generated by Wonder Wall's breakout game against Philly.

Think you had a rough week? Make that one win in five tries since Arenas' return ... and, yes, that was John Wall hobbling away from his first duel with D-Rose with his left foot in a boot after suffering a sprained arch.

The boot on his left foot isn't the only early obstacle to J-Wall's Rookie of the Year bid. Griffin's dunks and numbers are so irresistibly addictive that he can probably bank on half of the ROY votes even if the Clips go 1-81.

Wall is averaging 18.0 points, 9.1 assists and 2.6 steals ... numbers no rook has managed for an entire season. But we didn't expect Wall to miss five of his first 15 games while his ROY co-favorite in L.A. has missed none.

Our man Michael Lee of The Washington Post checks in from the Wizards' ongoing road woes (0-10) with a point we wish we'd made in the Weekend Dime: JaVale McGee improved a bunch just by trying out for Team USA.

We'd love to keep talking about JaVale McGee's continuing progress, but John Wall's stop/start rookie season -- in and out of the lineup thanks to foot and knee injuries -- and that 0-12 road record don't make it easy.

Finding a taker for Arenas before Christmas? Best Wiz week since they won the draft lottery in May. The euphoria, though, can last only so long when you're 0-13 on the road ... and with fears growing about Wall's knee.

December 2009: Arenas versus Crittenton. December 2010: McGee versus Blatche. December 2011: The Wiz obviously don't want to see a lockout, but that might be the only way to guarantee an incident-free Christmas.

Even with all the injury woes, J-Wall had four 25-point games before Jan. 1. Which is a major deal because that equals the total for Wiz rooks over the previous 25 seasons: Three for Googs in '92, one by A.J. English in '90.

The record for consecutive away L's to open the season was set when the 1992-93 Mavs started 0-29 on the road. The Wiz are up (down?) to 0-18 going into Thursday's must-win trip to Sota (not on TNT for some reason).

The numbers are distressing wherever you look. The Wiz will become the sixth team in history to start a season 0-20 on the road if they can't win Wednesday at Milwaukee ... and J-Wall is shooting 35.7 percent in January.

It's not just the fact that the Wiz are only the sixth team ever to start 0-20 on the road ... with the 1992-93 Mavs' record (0-29) perilously within range. It's that they've lost those 20 in a row by an average of 14.3 points.

The committee (of one) had an up-close seat for Wall's first exhibition game. Can't say, though, that we're overflowing with optimism about seeing Wall's first-ever NBA road win from the same seat Monday night.

My Wiz-loving boss obviously did not get to see road win No. 1 when he came to Dallas. Worse yet: I'm stealing from his Twitter feed in sharing that Wall's last regular-season road W came March 3, 2010 ... in Athens, Ga.

Don't want to spoil a momentous weekend for the Wiz, but their 0-25 start on the road will be remembered here as the more indefensible run of futility compared to Cleveland's, because of the two teams' rosters.

Can't quite co-sign on the jokes about the Wiz absorbing yet another road L when L.A.'s own Blake Griffin won the dunk contest over McGee. Not when Wall, instead of sharing it with Cousins, got solo MVP love in the rook game.

Hinrich's contract was salary dumped. Bibby's contract is about to be bought out. And owner Ted Leonsis just issued a letter of "transparency." From here, hopefully, we can put the down-the-stretch focus back on Wall.

It'd be nice, by season's end, if Wall can at least claim to be unanimously regarded as the season's second-best rookie. A second win to avoid tying the Kings' 1-40 record road disaster in 1990-91 wouldn't hurt, either.

Eleven road games to go. One more victory needed to avoid matching Sacramento's 1-40 road infamy in 1990-91. Friday in Toronto and the April 13 finale in Cleveland look like the most promising opportunities.

The grief Javale McGee got for his triple-double focused way too much on the cheap late bucket and not nearly enough on his 12 blocks. No one's swatted that many shots in one game since Keon Clark in March 2001.

So much for joking about how VCU should get the Wizards' spot. Never gave the Rams much thought beyond Eric Maynor and Larry Sanders, but I do know now they're not close enough to DC to attempt that regional reach.

We've been seduced by big April numbers from Blatche before. So let's keep the focus on the damage Jordan Crawford is doing and the trio of Wizards (Wall, McGee and Crawford) that have delivered triple-doubles.

Not even the league's worst road record, Wall's early injuries or the l-o-n-g wait to finally win three in a row can prevent us from scoring the season as a W for the Wiz, simply because they found a trade-taker for Arenas.

min.summary: You know how he feels about David Kahn. The #freekevinlove campaign suggests he's not the biggest Rambis fan, either. Maybe it all leads to Simmons being named Wolves coach and GM someday. Thoughts, Sota?

The sad Wolves are superlucky ESPN.com's daily automated rankings haven't started yet. Losing both ends of a back-to-back in Florida by 74 combined points would have dropped them out of Hollinger's top 30.

Love uncorks the first 30/30 game since Moses Malone's in 1982? Beasley follows up a 42-point shredding of Sacramento by hanging 35 on the Knicks? Next thing you know people will start saying Sota has a plan.
The D-League geek in me can't resist voicing unreserved support -- while acknowledging that nobody in basketball does this yet -- for the baseball-

The committee (of one) gets its first live look later this week at Sota's eclectic front-line triumvirate of K-Love, Beasley and Darko. We're probably more excited than we should be saying out loud, but -- oops. Too late.

Poor Sota. The young Wolves are only a month from having to face San Antonio twice in a span of three days (Jan. 9 and 11) after the Spurs just wiped out double-digit deficits on them twice in a span of nine days.

K-Love is bidding to become the first player to average 20-and-15 for an entire season since Moses Malone's MVP season of '82-83. He's also at a tidy .427 on 3s to distract us further from the Wolves' lead-blowing habit.

Gaudy as K-Love's numbers are getting, they can't mask Sota's record. An All-Star spot -- when the likes of Melo, Nowitzki and Duncan need the coaches' vote in the West -- will be the toughest thing he tries to snag.

The Metrodome's roof caves in. Then LeBron James publicly ponders an dispersal draft headlined by Kevin Love. Then Kobe Bryant slams the Wolves even harder with his ''Yeah, I said it'' shot. Some winter in Sota.

The Wolves are 70-210 since the KG trade for an NBA-low winning percentage of .250. The C's? An NBA-best .730 (203-75). Apologies, 'Sota: Had to bring it up with your kids in Boston on Monday. Even with KG out.

To the Wolves' issues with holding leads and executing in crunch time, add this unusual dilemma: Sota just went a whole calendar year -- yes, all of 2010 -- without winning a game in 15 tries against a NW Division foe.

The hardest thing to take for K-Love lovers praying that their guy sneaks onto the West squad for the All-Star Game is that the young Wolves' dismal record includes a league-high five L's after leading by 15 or more.

Remember up high where the Lakers, thanks to what Professor Hollinger rates as the league's weakest schedule so far, were dinged for playing just 13 games so far against .500 or better teams? 'Sota has already played 25.

Here's why the Wolves had to make a faux Kevin Love cologne commercial to doll up his All-Star bid: Only the winless Wiz have a worse road record than Sota's 2-22 mark, which includes 12 single-digit road defeats.

Move over, Hawks: Some week for the Wolves. Kevin Love just became their first post-KG All-Star, and Sota no longer leads the league in blown double-digit leads, eclipsed by the Kings and Wiz (10 to the Wolves' nine).

No time to savor those road wins in Houston and New Orleans. Not for Kevin Love. Not with LaMarcus Aldridge in Sota on Monday night, averaging 29.8 ppg and 8.4 rpg since Love was named as Yao's injury fill-in.

Two points and four boards in his All-Star bow didn't count. Kevin Love's run of 42 consecutive double-doubles continues, just eight shy of the longest such streak (Moses Malone's 50) since the NBA/ABA merger in '76-77.

His All-Star campaign was a success and his double-double streak rolls on, so what else is there this season for Kevin Love? Keeping the Wolves out of our basement now that the Cavs are uncorking the occasional big win.

This should give you a feel for the load Kevin Love has to carry: 'Sota is only 3-8 when Love rumbles for 20 points and 20 rebounds ... including 1-2 last week when he somehow did it in three straight road games.

The warmest consolation we can serve up after Kevin Love's double-double streak perished: The Wolves are in the throes of a 4-5 heat wave and just halted a run of 20 straight losses to divisional foes by throttling Utah.

A full week to digest it and even more unwanted time to think thanks to a groin injury won't help Love rationalize how his double-double streak perished against a team that gives up crazy stat lines for fun. Golden State?

As if the swirling speculation about his job and losing Love to a groin injury wasn't enough, Rambis' Wolves still have Chicago and Miami left in a seven-game stretch that also featured the Lakers, Mavs, Thunder and Celts.

Have we seen the last of Love in 2010-11? No sense asking him to play hurt with nothing at stake and when he clearly hasn't been the same Love in the last six games he did play, managing just 12.8 ppg and 9.2 rpg in that span.

The pertinent stats for another hard-to-watch season that had us longing for Rubio: Sota went 13-40 during Love's run of 53 straight double-doubles ... and now holds the league's longest playoff drought at six seasons.

tor.summary: The highlight of the Raptors' start was not their rout of Cleveland. Not to us. Not when Reggie Evans morphed into Dennis Rodman and totaled 30 rebounds -- with just two points -- in Toronto's opening two games.

Here's a capsule glimpse of early post-Bosh life north of the border: Jarrett Jack has been the last Raptor unveiled to Air Canada Centre-goers in pregame introductions in Toronto's first two home games.

Bosh might be gone, but you can't take this away from the Raps: No team in the East, after Friday night's stunner, has a better record in Orlando over the past five seasons than Toronto with its 5-3 mark. You can look it up.

Bosh's, uh, character-building November continues. Toronto is suddenly a sparkling 1-0 against mighty Boston since his departure. The Raps, with Bosh, had lost their previous six home dates with the Celts dating to 2007.

Losing the Rodman-esque rebounding of Reggie Evans also robs the Raps of their biggest post-Bosh personality ... but we'll get by on more of the brief flurries of 3s (and resultant ovations) Peja has delivered so far.

More surprised that seven of the teams occupying the East's eight playoff spots as of Monday morning sported records of .500 or better? Or that the Bosh-less Raps were No. 8 at a pretty respectable 8-12? Raps for me.

All it took was one big comeback against Detroit, helped along by Jerryd Bayless' big 31-point breakout, for the Raps to say they've enjoyed post-trade life more than the Hornets, who are 4-8 since Jarrett Jack's arrival.

Beating the Lakers without Bargnani, Evans and Peja would have required a miracle, even with the helpful 1 p.m. Sunday tipoff, but the Raps are still borderline overachieving given their collective youth and ill health.

Are we already down to nine teams for the East's eight playoff spots? Don't enjoy hitting our Canadian pals with such cold truths, but we see no one -- starting with the Raps at No. 10 -- who can realistically make a move.

The Mavs were Dirk-less, but Toronto -- also on the second night of a back-to-back -- had no Bargnani, Calderon, Evans or Peja and lost Kleiza (ejection) and Bayless (ankle) in the second half. We're still tipping our hat.

Two games out of No. 8 in the East with all those injuries? The Raps will take it. And there's always this when No. 8 is out of reach: They need just one 3 in 21 more games for 1,000 games in a row with at least one triple.

Can this Canada lover get away with focusing on the fact that Jose Calderon recently joined Steve Nash in the exclusive two-man club of point guards with more than one 20-point, 15-assist game this season? Didn't think so.

The bad news? Toronto has replaced Phoenix as the NBA's new No. 30 in defensive efficiency. The consolation? I've seen multiple tweets about it, suggesting genuine south-of-the-border concern about the Raps' fortunes.

You hesitate, on one hand, to say that our Raps have hit rock bottom. On the other hand? They just lost to Sota after 12 straight Ws over the Wolves and also lost their famed streak after 986 straight games with at least one 3.

From @derekgbell on Twitter came the reminder that our Raps -- doing very little these days beyond getting DeRozan and Amir Johnson some prime-time run -- have beaten Boston, Dallas, Orlando and OKC. Somehow.

It's been a lean 2011 to say the least for our friends north of the border. The Raps have a mere four wins in 23 tries in 2011 ... and those four victims (Cavs, Kings, Wolves and Clips) have a composite record of 55-159.

Is Canada big enough for two Italian forwards who don't do much board work? You needn't ponder that one too deeply. Latest word is that Gallinari isn't available and that the Raps are not so hot to pair him with Bargnani.

Didn't feel good putting the Raps at No. 30 last week. Didn't feel right inflicting the sort of pain I know it caused our Canadian pals. Thankfully the Raps went out and stunned Chicago to ensure it was a one-week injustice.

You buy the London factor with Lopez because his overall line was so gaudy. Bargnani? Twelve rebounds to go with 35 points feels like more of a three-OT effect, since he needed 52 minutes to grab that dozen.

It's borderline common knowledge that the post-LeBron Cavs started 7-9 before their epic unraveling. So how did we get to Week 20 before noting that the post-Bosh Raps started 8-11 and cratered similarly?

What is it about the Southwest that so agrees with Team Canada? First it was a Dec. 28 shocker in Dallas. Then Sunday's stunner in OKC to give the Raps their first back-to-back W's since the 18th/19th games of the season.

Something tells me you weren't terribly surprised -- even after their seemingly miraculous win at OKC as recently as March 20 -- that the Raps followed up that stunner with road L's to the Nuggets, Suns, Dubs and Clips.

Make that two wins over Orlando to go with an improbable season sweep of the Thunder as well as wins over Dallas (road) and Chicago (home). So give the Raptors this much: When they do win, it's almost always an event.

My apologies, Canada. The Raps will head for the summer having left this Toronto wannabe with the sense that Bargnani's underwhelming season as a first option is the far bigger deal, sadly, than DeRozan's progress.

cha.summary: Didn't totally believe it when someone told me, but the frustrated Bobcats -- despite posting just one winning season in their six-season existence -- had never started 0-3 before. Not until this turnover-ridden start.

Just to make it clear how new owner Michael Jordan saw things before the Bobs' disheartening start, via the Charlotte Business Journal: "We've got to make the playoffs. ... Anything less than that is a step backwards."

Humbling as it is to be quoting editors, what can I say? Our own Royce Webb had a better Twitter reaction than me to Charlotte, despite Nazr's second-ever 20/20, falling to 0-4 at home: "Buyer's remorse yet, MJ?"

We always get on MJ when he's not visible, but it's hard to quibble with Saturday night's absence. First home game that His Airness wasn't sitting courtside ... and S-Jax uncorks the first triple-double in team history.

The next team they beat with a record of .500 or better will be the first. The Bobs are 0-8 against that group -- including last week's two momentum-crushing losses to the Knicks -- and 6-3 against sub-.500 teams.

Updating the pertinent numbers in Charlotte: 6-4 against teams with losing records, 1-9 against teams with winning records and six technical fouls already for Stephen Jackson, just one shy of Melo's league-leading seven.

Bobcats castoffs Tyson Chandler and Raymond Felton are flying. The Bobcats still in Charlotte rank 12th in defensive efficiency compared to No. 1 last season. You can imagine how well Larry Brown is taking all this.

Raymond Felton is playing better than ever as a Knick. Dirk says Tyson Chandler has had a KG-type impact on Dallas' D. Add it up and you start to wonder how soon the Michael Jordan-for-Executive of the Year jokes start.

Have to believe the following Stephen Jackson gem, so soon after Barkley's unforgettable ''He's the engine that stirs the drink'' scouting report on Rondo, clinched Larry Brown's ouster: ''We're just terrible on all cylinders.''

Only with his fourth team -- after coaching the Clips, Hornets and Cavs -- does Paul Silas know how it feels to start 2-0. Then came a one-point L to a Golden State team that doesn't win close games to halt the honeymoon.

You still have to expect trades out of the Bobcats -- maybe Stephen Jackson goes, maybe it's Gerald Wallace -- but the interim product is a lot more watchable under Paul Silas. As in 7.4 points per game more watchable.

We know they've played faster and freer since Silas took over. The home wins over Memphis and Chicago to start last week, however, were the first W's of real quality in the Silas era, aided by the return of G-Wallace.

The Mikecats' next six games are on the road -- with the first five out West -- and Miami/Dallas/Boston are lined up for their first three games back home. The winning record under Silas, in other words, is under threat.

Charles Oakley for Assistant Coach of the Year? The much-maligned Kwame Brown, with Oak riding him, has two games this month with at least 13 points and 15 boards ... after totaling one in the previous four seasons.

Can't call the Mikecats boring when they've played a league-high 22 games decided by five points or fewer. Yet you also can't help but wonder how much higher they'd be in the East if they weren't 10-12 in those games.

A glimpse of Michael Jordan on the practice floor? Stephen Jackson with a buzzer-beater that gets all of us reciting his signature "I make love to pressure" line? Has there ever been a sexier week in Bobcats history?

The vibe was so upbeat before the break when all the focus was on Michael Jordan at practice. Now? The prodigal Bobcat and their only All-Star ever -- Gerald Wallace -- is being shopped at the deadline. Without success.

Remember how MJ could score even when he drove 1-on-5? The 1-on-29 sport of team building is another sport entirely, given what little His Airness managed to get back for Felton, G-Wallace and Tyson Chandler.

Breaking up a going-nowhere team might actually prove to be the right move. Yet something tells me MJ would have had some issues with his bosses if he were on the team dumping Chandler, Felton and G-Wallace.

Good one from Hollinger: Even with three teams "battling" for No. 8 in the East -- Charlotte among them despite the G-Wallace salary dump -- we might see our worst playoff team since Boston got in at 35-47 in '94-95.

How down is the bottom half of the East? MJ's Bobcats salary-dumped G-Wallace and already have three losses more than they had last season ... and yet they still haven't dropped out of the race for the No. 8 slot.

The "race" for No. 8 in the East in a nutshell: Losing nine of their first 11 games in March couldn't knock the Bobs out. Instead? Weekend wins over the Celtics and Knicks make them the "hot" team in this "race."

The "race" for No. 8 in the East is such that the Bobs can't protest too loudly if we focus on our man Matty Carroll's 26 points Sunday night.  Not after Carroll's breakout was wasted in a must-win home date with the Wiz.

Making the playoffs, even in the East, was realistically impossible after trading G-Wallace and losing S. Jackson. But to hang in for so long and then eliminate themselves with back-to-back L's to the Wiz and Cavs ... ugh.

phi.summary: Elias says that the last (and only) Doug Collins-coached team that started 0-3 -- Detroit in 1995-96 -- won its next three games. Philly's next three foes? Washington away, followed by Indiana and Cleveland at home.

Despite four straight 20-point games from Brand -- his longest such streak since April 2007 -- folks in Philly already have dialed down the playoff talk. Year 1 under Collins and Thorn is suddenly an "audition season."

Calls for Iguodala to be dealt will only get louder if the Sixers continue to struggle, since Iguodala does have admirers in other cities and since the resulting daylight for Evan Turner could only be a good thing. Right?

Iguodala's future is still the story with this team ... even after that New Orleans trade with Toronto that cost the Hornets an asset (Peja's contract) believed to be earmarked for an Iguodala offer. Just tellin' the truth.

Funny thing about Philly: The same team beaten twice in overtime by the Wiz has cruised by double-digits in all four of its rare victories. Must be why Hollinger's rankings treat the Jrue Holiday Sixers kinder than we do.

As stated via Twitter on a very sad Friday night, Phil Jasner of the Philly Daily News was as synonymous with the Sixers as Dr. J, Iverson, you name it. So please, Sixers: Sew something onto your unis to pay tribute to him.

The good news: My buddy Scooter's beloved Jodie Meeks is raining in 3s after being stuck on the inactive list for the first six games. The bad news: Meeks' splash means No. 2 pick Evan Turner is coming off the bench.

One theory to explain the 8-3 revival beyond help from the schedule and Philly's  vastly improved D: Opposing teams can't lock in on the Sixers because even they aren't sure night-to-night where their O will come from.

An eight-game road trip actually starts to sound pretty good when you go to Orlando right after it trades away half the team ... and when you go to Denver and Melo doesn't play ... and when a blizzard strikes back home.

Even without Iguodala, Philly can finish 4-4 on that monster eight-game trip if it can steal a win Monday night in New Orleans ... against the same Hornets who scored 23 points in the first half at Philly on Dec. 12.

Brand quietly has twice as many double-doubles (14) as he did last season. Another attempt to take Doug Collins' mind off that painful donation in Detroit: Philly has won 9 of 11 at home after going 12-29 in 2009-10.

If the Sixers end up missing out on the playoffs, they'll know exactly where to point for Culprit No. 1: Philly is 2-8 in games decided by five points or fewer. And Charlotte and Milwaukee still look capable of capitalizing.

More crunch-time pain: Philly's losses to Orlando and Charlotte marked the first time since January 1998 that the Sixers lost games on consecutive days after leading in the last two minutes of the fourth quarter in both.

Can't tell you how often I've heard it from rival coaches/scouts: Collins has the Sixers, for all of their issues in close games (1-7 in games decided by three or less) and suspect shooting, playing as hard as anyone does.

How unglamorous is the group that Collins came back to coaching for? Philly was one of just three teams, alongside Charlotte and Cleveland, without a single player listed in the final results of All-Star fan balloting.

Now we know who the Spurs fear most in the NBA Finals after the surging Sixers held them to 71 points Friday night. You have to go back five seasons, all the way to 2006-07, for San Antonio's last victory in Philly.

At 6-3 in February, Philly needs only one more win in the next week to clinch its third successive winning month. Which hasn't happened since the 2000-01 dream season, when the Sixers went to the Finals and AI was MVP.

Collins is a factor in the main COY race now and has East Coach of the Month for February wrapped up. The Sixers went 9-3, passing .500 for the first time all season with their best month since February 2003 (8-2).

LeBron, Rondo, Westbrook ... and the rejuvenated Iguodala. That's your full list of players who've racked up three triple-doubles this season, with two of Iguodala's coming in the flying Sixers' past two games.

Even the most hardened Philly fan might forgive the Milwaukee debacle when they read this: Only Chicago has a better record in the Eastern Conference since Feb. 1, at 14-4, than the Sixers' 13-6 mark in that span.

Gonna be very, very interesting if the Sixers indeed wind up facing Miami in Round 1. They need to play small and run to win -- two truths that theoretically help Miami -- but they defend much better than the Knicks.

Something tells me Philly, after feeling sneaky good about the potential Miami matchup in Round 1, wouldn't mind seeing the Heat move up to No. 2 after surrendering 71 points to LeBron and D-Wade on Friday night.

Only the Thibodeau Bulls have improved more since last season than Doug Collins' Sixers. Yet the immediate focus in Philly, I'm afraid, has to be on the recent defensive slippage and iffy health of Iguodala and Lou Williams.

In addition to the Collins factor, credit generally good health for putting Philly on the brink of its first winning season since 2004-05. The flip side: Going 2-8 in OT games didn't make Doug's job any easier.

det.summary: Even we figured seeing themselves parked at No. 30 last Monday would be the low point of the Pistons' week. Then came L's to the Nets and OKC by a combined three points and that 34-9 fourth quarter in Chicago.

Let the record show the game that put a halt to the Pistons' full-on descent into crisis -- Friday's win over Charlotte -- came with a certain Tracy McGrady starting at point guard after the benching of young Stuckey.

Props to the Pistons, especially Kuester. They've been presented with some winnable games since the 0-5 start, true, but it wasn't long ago that you didn't like their chances against anyone because of all the turmoil.

It's one of the untold surprises of the season: Detroit is firmly in the heart of the best-of-the-worst battle for seeds No. 6 through No. 8 in the East, despite that 0-5 start and the player-coach tensions that won't go away.

No matter what you think of what's left of his own game at this point, T-Mac's views on the "terrible" compatibility of the LeBron/D-Wade tag team in Miami are relevant, candid and irresistible comment fodder.

Sunday's visit from the cowering Cavs was certainly welcome, but I wonder whether Detroiters would be happier if the rumors were true about the rich Qataris who won the 2022 World Cup bid wanting to buy the Pistons.

What's worse than the Pistons' no-show in the committee's presence in a half-empty building in New Orleans? They blew a 25-point lead at home against Toronto, wasting Big Ben's 23-point, 14-board eruption.

Tay Prince's come-and-get-me game (28 points/12 boards/8 dimes in an OT win over New Orleans) sealed the Pistons' second W of the week over a winning team. Last Monday? They were 0-11 against the .500-or-better set.

Would prefer to be telling you precisely when Tayshaun or Rip might finally be traded. The only predictions we can comfortably make, though, involve the Pistons' Sunday home games: Four already have gone to OT.

Only four players ever have scored 40 on New Year's Eve: Wilt, MJ, Quentin Richardson and T-Mac. So what happens to T-Mac's Pistons in PHX? First team in 389 games (you can look it up) to score only 75 against the Suns.

Don't need to wait for the trade to be completed to point out that the Pistons, just through their willingness to put Rip Hamilton into the Melo deal for cap relief, are finally admitting that keeping Rip around is a bad idea.

It still hasn't quite sunk in, no matter how much time these molasses-slow trade talks have provided, that the former powerhouse that could have drafted Melo is now an up-for-sale third team facilitating a Melo trade.

If they can hold Phoenix to 75 points in the midst of the daily Rip-versus-Kuester drama, don't we have to give the Pistons more of a shot to sneak into the No. 8 spot in the East than most of these stragglers in the hunt?

Addendum: If they can hold Phoenix to 75 points and then win in Orlando in the midst of all this Rip-versus-Kuester drama -- with a dash of Tayshaun static -- you can't rule the Pistons out of playoff contention. Yet.

T-Mac reincarnated as a PG? Rip out of the doghouse after 13 games in exile? The Pistons are suddenly full of surprises ... although Rip's return is an unspoken admission that a trade by the deadline is a huge long shot.

Closer to a sale of the Pistons than we've been all season? Sure seems like it. Closer to a resolution on Rip Hamilton's future after he was freed from exile to play in exactly one game? Your guess is as good as ours.

The Pistons have convinced pretty much everyone around the league that they're serious about keeping Tayshaun Prince. The problem? Finding a taker for Rip Hamilton was their far bigger goal of Trade Deadline Week.

After the shootaround boycott, where did you think they'd end up? No matter how much Kuester has contributed to this, insubordination to that degree pretty much clinched Detroit's trip to the basement.

You actually can lump the Pistons together with the Heat even though they've been engulfed by distinctly different brands of chaos: They're the only two teams this season to squander a lead of at least 20 points twice.

Rip Hamilton is starting again in Detroit. Except that his first start since Dec. 17 came on the road in Denver, so we await the reception he gets Wednesday night back in Detroit should Rip get the start against Toronto.

The same Rip Hamilton so many of us thought would never play for the Pistons again just averaged 19.8 ppg on 52 percent shooting in the four games before a family bereavement forced him out of the lineup Friday.

Only because my oldest (Alexander The Greatest) is inexplicably such a big Jerebko fan do I divert the focus away from Detroit's dysfunction to ask if you like the Monroe-Daye-Jerebko (when healthy) trio's promise.

So much for the notion that the post-mutiny Pistons could quietly inch to the finish line. Stuckey's benching in Sunday's L to Boston was for -- you guessed it -- ignoring Kuester's call to re-enter the previous L vs. Chicago.

Remember Kuester's 1-27 season coaching collegiately at George Washington? This chaos-filled season of player rebellion had to be rougher, all the way down to the Pistons not being sold until the season's final week.

lac.summary: Last week's two questions, about the state of Griffin and Baron, have been replaced by one nagging new question about the collective unit: How can the Clips look so ready to surrender so early? After three games?

This is the third successive season the Clips have started 0-4. Have to point out, though, that they haven't played anyone with a losing record yet and start this week with a back-to-back in New Orleans and San Antonio.

Baron Davis has logged only 10 minutes of court time in the Clips' past five games. The Clips lost all five. Conclusion: They'll need more than one scapegoat if they can't stay ahead of Sota in the actual standings or here.

The committee's old friend Scott Howard-Cooper of NBA.com summed it up on Twitter better than we could: "Worse than the record itself is the fact the last five Ls came against the Knicks, Pacers, Wolves, Nets and Pistons."

When Vinny Del Negro said he didn't regret taking the Clippers job after a 1-13 start, it didn't take too many guesses to pinpoint why: If you have to leave Derrick Rose's side, Blake Griffin ain't a bad rebound rook.

Did Gordon's ongoing struggles from 3 and the Clips' hideous start lead to a too-harsh snub in the Weekend Dime? I still say he can't be higher than sixth on that five-man list ... but I feel shame for not mentioning him.

A new low for a team that has seen a few: Never in the Clippers' 33 seasons -- or the preceding eight seasons in Buffalo, for that matter -- had they lost two in a row by one before last week's LÂs to the Lakers and Griz.

Blake Griffin and his Clips finally won a couple road games, but the breakthroughs in Detroit and Chicago made you wonder: Shouldn't they actually play better when they're farther away from their heckling owner?

With a hat tip to LA Times sage Mark Heisler: It's getting to the point, with or without this little 4-1 uptick, that we have to start seriously asking how many players on the planet are more exciting than Blake Griffin, if any?

The Clips are 6-7 since Kaman last played, with Blake Griffin and Eric Gordon accounting for nearly 50 percent of L.A.'s points during that span. More evidence, in other words, that I still owe Gordon an apology or three.

The Clippers will have the most interesting Angeleno at All-Star Weekend. The Clippers have a guy so watchable that the anchor on almost every highlight invites you to just ignore their record. The Clippers, people.

They're 13-12 since that 1-13 start. They just beat the Heat and the Lakers in the space of five days. They'll have the Angeleno, we say again, gawked at more than any other at L.A.'s All-Star Weekend. The Clips, people.

Stealing this idea from the New York Post's Peter Vecsey because it was too tantalizing for a lifelong Braves fan to resist: Move the Clips back to Buffalo now to ensure that Blake Superior's rim assaults make the playoffs.

Let's keep it positive until the upcoming schedule, combined with Gordon's wrist injury, leaves us no choice. Blake's Clips are 13-7 in their last 20 games ... with eight straight home wins for the first time since (whoa) 1993.

Eleven road games in a row? Some of Blake's dunks seem more plausible than a road trip that long, which should be great for all those fan bases thirsting for a glimpse, but sure death to the Clips' faint playoff dreams.

Haven't heard exactly why the Clips' Grammys Road Trip is 11 games and the Lakers' Grammys Trip is seven ... but sympathy fades quickly after back-to-back losses in Cleveland and Toronto. Even with Gordon still out.

Good spot by ESPN The Magazine's Molly Knight: Blake Griffin has about 208,000 followers on Twitter. The Clippers' team feed has about 28,000 followers. Sounds like an appropriate representation of the situation.

There actually has been a longer road trip than the 11-gamer (2-9) just endured by the Clips. The Detroit Falcons went 3-10 on a 13-game excursion in 1946-47. The 11-gamer is tied for second-longest in history.

Goal for the final 19 games? With Gordon freshly reinjured, Blake might as well go for the 16 double-doubles he needs to surpass Shaq's 68 in 1992-93, which is the rookie record since the NBA/ABA merger in 1976-77.

The Clips went a league-worst 2-12 in February without Eric Gordon. This month? With Gordon playing only twice and Mo Williams at the point, L.A. would be 6-0 if it didn't blow a 20-point lead in New Jersey.

Ease up on Blake about those seven straight games without a double-double. I'd say that the 30, 8 and 8 he rung up Saturday, after those scary pregame scenes at Staples, suggest he's coping with the grind just fine.

The romantic in me wants to believe that this is a playoff team if Gordon hadn't missed 26 games (during which the Clips went 7-19). But the realist in me shouts back with reminders about L.A.'s weak bench and 1-13 start.

There's something about knowing you're just a few days away from seeing Blake throw down live, even in an otherwise meaningless game, that makes you giddy to type the words even on a Monday morning. On no sleep.

Knowing how uber-competitive he is, something tells me Blake -- after 62 double-doubles and 210 dunks -- ain't gonna be happy when he finds out his Clips are tied for the league's No. 2 playoff drought (five seasons).
